units.title: Reading written Russian closely: argument, register, subjectless sentences and compressed clauses

lessons.title: Reading a short argumentative passage: the claim, its support, and the author's stance
lessons.explanation: A Russian paragraph that argues something is not a random string of sentences. It has a small number of load-bearing parts, and once you can name them you can read a real page of Russian prose rather than guessing. The parts are: a claim (тезис, TYE-zees), the support offered for it, a concession or counter-move, and a conclusion or recommendation (вывод, VY-vat). Russian marks these parts with a small set of discourse signals — однако (ad-NA-ka, however), во-первых (va-PYER-vykh, firstly), во-вторых (va-fta-RYKH, secondly), следовательно (SLYE-da-va-tyel-na, consequently), поэтому (pa-EH-ta-moo, that is why) — and these signals are the cheapest and most reliable map you have. Cornell's grammar makes a point that matters here: 'When you read mature Russian prose, with its long sentences and variety of word-orders, you have to keep your eyes peeled for these elements and recognize what type of sentence you're dealing with.' The elements it means are predicates — verbs, short adjectives, and predicatives — because Russian can build a complete sentence on any of the three, and a long sentence may contain no ordinary subject-plus-verb core at all. Two further facts from linguistics shape how you read. First, a text is not just a chain of grammatical sentences; text linguistics treats 'texts as communication systems', which means the unit you are interpreting is the whole argument, not the sentence. Second, cohesion — 'the grammatical and lexical linking within a text or sentence that holds a text together and gives it meaning' — is what tells you which sentence belongs to which claim. In Russian, the linking devices you will actually see are repeated nouns, demonstratives such as этот (EH-tat, this) and такой (ta-KOY, such), and the conjunctions above. The practical discipline is this. Read the paragraph once without translating a single word. Mark every signal word. Ask three questions: what is being asserted, what is offered in its support, and where does the writer signal their own evaluation? Then translate, sentence by sentence, and check each sentence against the answer to those questions. Learners who translate first and interpret second routinely produce a summary of the words of a paragraph rather than of its argument. Two more words belong to this routine. An абзац (ab-ZATS) is a paragraph, the unit you actually work on, and основная мысль (as-nav-NA-ya mysl) is the main idea, which is not the same object as the тезис: the main idea is what the paragraph is about, and the claim is what it asks you to accept. Confusing the two is the commonest failure at this stage, because a paragraph can have a clear main idea and a badly supported claim.
lessons.example: Here is a short teaching passage written for this lesson; it is an authored model text, not a quotation. В последние годы многие компании переводят сотрудников на удалённую работу. Сторонники этой практики утверждают, что она экономит время на дорогу. Однако, во-первых, не всякую работу можно делать дома, а во-вторых, дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха. Поэтому, по мнению авторов отчёта, удалённая работа подходит не всем. (v pas-LYED-nee-ye GO-dy MNO-gee-ye kam-PA-nee pee-ree-VO-dyat so-TROOD-nee-kaf na oo-da-LYON-noo-yoo ra-BO-too. sta-RON-nee-kee EH-tay PRAK-tee-kee oot-veerzh-DA-yut, shto a-NA e-ka-NO-meet VRYE-mya na da-RO-goo. ad-NA-ka, va-PYER-vykh, nye FSYA-koo-yoo ra-BO-too MOZH-na DYE-lat DO-ma, a va-fta-RYKH, DO-ma TROOD-na at-dee-LEET ra-BO-too at OTD-dy-kha. pa-EH-ta-moo, pa MNYE-nee-yoo AF-ta-raf at-CHYO-ta, oo-da-LYON-na-ya ra-BO-ta pad-KHO-deet nye VSYEM.) Now read it the slow way. Sentence one (В последние годы... на удалённую работу) has no argument; it sets the scene with a plural-object imperfective verb, переводят, 'they are transferring', describing a general trend. Sentence two names the claim-holders — сторонники (sta-RON-nee-kee, supporters) — and the claim itself, inside a что-clause after утверждать (oot-veerzh-DAT, to assert): remote work saves travel time. Sentence three is the pivot: однако (ad-NA-ka, however) announces that the writer is not neutral, and во-первых/во-вторых open a two-part objection. Sentence four is the conclusion, and it is signalled twice — поэтому plus по мнению авторов отчёта (pa MNYE-nee-yoo AF-ta-raf at-CHYO-ta), 'according to the authors of the report', which is a hedging attribution, not the writer's own voice. So the extractable argument is: the trend is real; its supporters make a saving claim; the report's authors concede nothing but object on two grounds and conclude that the practice does not suit everyone. Notice what is NOT the argument: the fact that remote work exists, or that some people like it. The lexical items you needed were тезис (the claim), доказательства (da-ka-ZA-tyel-stva, the supporting evidence) and вывод (the conclusion).
lessons.question: In the passage above, which element tells you that the author of the text is reporting someone else's evaluation rather than asserting their own claim?
lessons.answer: По мнению авторов отчёта — 'according to the opinion of the authors of the report' — which hands the conclusion to an external source.
lessons.distractor: Поэтому — 'that is why' — because a causal connector always marks reported speech.
lessons.correction: Therefore-words (поэтому, следовательно) connect a reason to a result; they say nothing about whose voice the result belongs to. The attribution is the phrase по мнению (pa MNYE-nee-yoo) plus a genitive source, авторов отчёта. If you delete it, the writer owns the conclusion; with it, the writer only reports it. This is exactly the distinction a close reading is supposed to recover, and it is invisible if you translate the sentence as a flat statement of fact.

depth.definitions: Claim (тезис) is the proposition the writer wants you to accept. Support (доказательство) is whatever is offered to make the claim credible — in this passage, a saving in travel time. Concession is a move that grants something before objecting. Discourse signal is a small word whose job is to label the relation between two stretches of text: однако (contrast), во-первых/во-вторых (enumeration), поэтому (result), следовательно (consequence). Predicate is the part of a clause that asserts something; Russian allows verbs, short adjectives and predicatives to do this job. Cohesion is the grammatical and lexical linking that holds a text together. Attribution is language that assigns a statement to a source rather than to the writer. Prerequisite: you should already recognise что-clauses (lesson 76) and the predicative sentence types used in lessons 62 and 69.
depth.mechanism: Reading for argument works because writers do not distribute information evenly: they spend one sentence on the claim and several on support, and they use connectives to control how you weigh what follows. The mechanism is therefore a search, not a translation. First, scan for connective density: a stretch with однако, во-первых and поэтому is doing argumentative work, while a stretch of repeated imperfective verbs with каждый день is doing background. Second, find the sentence that could stand alone as the writer's point; every other sentence either supports it, qualifies it or reports someone else about it. Third, check the verb of reporting. Verbs such as утверждать ('to assert'), считать ('to consider'), and the phrase по мнению ('according to the opinion of') mark a stance as somebody's, and Russian uses them constantly in exactly the positions where English prose would use a subordinate clause. The limitation is real: Russian academic writing also lets a writer slide from reported to asserted position without any marker, and a single paragraph cannot settle authorship of a claim — you need the surrounding sentences. Note too that the Cornell sentence-type material is a reading aid, not a key to argument: knowing that a clause is predicative tells you where the assertion lives, not whether it is the writer's.
depth.secondExample: Take a deliberately non-argumentative paragraph and watch the same reading routine find nothing. Вчера я была в новом офисе. Офис большой и светлый, на стене висят часы, а на столах стоят компьютеры. Около окна стоит кулер с водой. В углу лежат коробки. (fchee-RA ya by-LA v NO-vam A-fee-sye. A-fees bal-SHOY ee SVYET-lyy, na stye-NYE vee-SYAT cha-SY, a na sta-LAKH sta-YAT kam-PYOO-te-ry. O-ka-la ak-NA sta-EET KOO-lyer s va-DOY. v oog-LOO lye-ZHAT ka-ROB-kee.) (Yesterday I was in the new office. The office is big and bright, there is a clock on the wall and there are computers on the desks. Next to the window there is a water cooler. There are boxes in the corner.) There is no тезис here, no therefore and no attribution, and the position verbs стоить and лежать (lesson 68) simply place objects in space. This is description, and the reading task for description is different: you track location and existence, and the assertive content is limited to 'these things are there'. Contrasting the two passages is the fastest way to feel the difference between prose that argues and prose that arranges.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is treating however as a mere pause. A learner reads Однако, во-первых... as 'and also, first...', loses the pivot, and then summarises the passage as agreeing with the supporters of remote work — the opposite of what it says. The diagnostic is mechanical: wherever you meet однако, несмотря на, хотя or тем не менее, the writer is about to disagree with something that precedes the marker, so the preceding claim is not the writer's. A second error is to read во-первых as 'for the first time' (the first-time sense belongs to a different construction entirely) or to expect a third item after во-вторых. A third error is to treat по мнению as filler; it is the strongest signal of transferred responsibility in the sentence.
depth.application: Task: take the remote-work passage, cover the last sentence, and write three English sentences — the claim, the two objections, and the conclusion — with no more than twenty words total. Then write a fourth sentence naming who owns each part. Model response: 'Trend: firms move staff to remote work. Objections: not all work can be done at home; home blurs work and rest. Conclusion: remote work does not suit everyone. Voice: the claim belongs to сторонники; the objections and conclusion belong to the report's authors, who present themselves through по мнению.' Self-review rubric: (1) did you keep the two objections separate and in the order the signals give them? (2) did you mark the attribution rather than absorbing it into the writer's voice? (3) did you avoid importing words that are not in the Russian? Score each yes/no; a pass needs three yes answers. Then repeat the whole routine on a fresh paragraph of your own choosing.
depth.summary: Argument reading is a decomposition skill. You reduce a Russian paragraph to four slots — claim, support, concession, conclusion — and you use connective density and attribution phrases to assign each slot a voice. What transfers is the routine: signal-scan first, translation second, decomposition third, restatement last. It works on essays, on news analysis and on any report in который-clause-heavy written style, and it is the prerequisite for the summary work in lesson 89, where you will produce the same decomposition out loud.

visual.title: Five-step close-reading routine over one paragraph
visual.description: A labelled sequence of five stages applied to the remote-work paragraph, each stage naming what to look for and what to write down. Rendered as text steps, not as video or animation.
steps: Stage 1 — Signal scan. Re-read with a pencil and circle only: однако, во-первых, во-вторых, поэтому, по мнению. Do not translate. Output: a list of markers with their sentence positions.
Stage 2 — Sentence typing. For each sentence decide whether it is background (repeated or imperfective verbs, time phrases), claim, support, or conclusion. Output: a one-word label per sentence.

Stage 3 — Voice check. Wherever a reporting verb or an attribution phrase appears (утверждать, по мнению, авторы отчёта), write the name of the owner next to the clause it governs. Output: a claim-to-owner mapping.
Stage 4 — Compression. Write the claim, the support and the conclusion in your own language, at most twenty words total. Output: the compressed skeleton.
Stage 5 — Verification. Return to the Russian and check every word of your compression against the text; delete anything you cannot point to. Output: a skeleton you could defend sentence by sentence.

lessons.title: Written register and spoken register: the same content, two grammars
lessons.explanation: Russian is unusual among the languages you know in how sharply its written and spoken registers are separated by grammar rather than only by vocabulary. Cornell states the split in one line about deverbals: 'Most deverbal forms occur primarily in written Russian, although the short forms of past passive participles and the present deverbal adverbs also occur in conversational style.' The same page compresses the whole relationship into an equation: 'Written style participles = Conversational style который clauses.' That is a usable rule of thumb, not a stylistic preference. Спoken Russian prefers a relative clause with который (ka-TO-ryy, which) and a finite verb; written Russian prefers a participle packed in front of the noun. Register itself is a defined notion in linguistics. 'In sociolinguistics, a register is a variety of language used for a particular purpose or particular communicative situation.' What makes register legally interesting is that it is conventionalised: a learner who masters the grammar of one register and uses it in the other will be understood and will still sound wrong. This lesson gives you a small set of markers that flip a sentence from spoken to written, so you can read both and choose deliberately. The markers are these. Lexical: книжный стиль (KNEESH-nyy steel, the bookish style) versus разговорный стиль (raz-ga-VOR-nyy steel, the conversational style). Word-formation: отглагольные существительные (verbal nouns) and participles mark written prose; verbs, particles and короткие add-ons mark speech. Syntactic: written Russian tolerates the double-negative-of-nothing style chain of genitives after a deverbal noun, and piles modifiers before the noun; spoken Russian unpacks the same content into two clauses with a shared subject. Pragmatic: written Russian names sources formally — данный (DAN-nyy, the given, the present), вышеуказанный (VY-she-oo-KA-zan-nyy, the aforementioned), в соответствии с (v sa-at-VYET-stvee s, in accordance with), в связи с (v SVYA-zee s, in connection with) — while spoken Russian uses pronouns and наверное-style hedges you already have from lesson 77. For reading, the practical consequence is a translation reflex. When you meet a participle or a verbal noun, expand it in your head into the corresponding который-clause or a clause with поэтому, recover the subject, then translate. When you meet the written formulaic frame, replace it with the plain word before translating: данный отчёт is просто этот отчёт, and в соответствии с решением is по решению. Three adjectives complete the vocabulary of the split. Устный (OOST-nyy) means oral or spoken, письменный (PEES-myen-nyy) means written, and официальный (a-fee-tsee-AL-nyy) means official or formal; the third is not a synonym of the other two, since an official document may be read aloud and remain official. And тем не менее (tyem nye MYE-nye-ye, nevertheless) is the written counterpart of the spoken но, so read it as a signal that a contrast is coming rather than as decoration.
lessons.example: Compare one fact written twice. Spoken version: Мы получили письмо, в котором было написано, что ремонт начнётся через месяц. (my pa-loo-CHEE-lee pees-MO, v ka-TO-rom BY-la na-PEE-sa-na, shto ree-MONT nach-NYOT-sya CHYE-ryez MYE-syats.) — 'We received a letter in which it was written that the repair would begin in a month.' Written version of the same content: В полученном письме сообщается о начале ремонта через месяц. (v pa-loo-CHEN-nom pees-MYE sa-ap-SHCHA-yet-sya a na-CHA-lee ree-MON-ta CHYE-ryez MYE-syats.) — 'The letter received reports the start of the repair in a month.' Read the two side by side and count the changes. One: письмо, в котором было написано, что becomes полученном письме — the который-clause collapses into a past passive participle (полученный, pa-loo-CHEN-nyy, received) which is then put in the prepositional case to agree with its noun. Two: the finite verb было написано is replaced by an impersonal-present verb сообщается (sa-ap-SHCHA-yet-sya, it is reported). Three: the clause начнётся ремонт becomes a verbal noun phrase o начале ремонта (a na-CHA-lee ree-MON-ta, about the beginning of the repair), and the future tense disappears entirely — the deverbal noun carries the event with no tense at all. Four: two clauses became one. Now reverse the reflex deliberately. Faced with В связи с увеличением числа сотрудников, работающих удалённо, было принято решение о реорганизации отдела. (v SVYA-zee s oo-vee-lee-CHE-nee-em CHIS-la so-TROOD-nee-kaf, ra-BO-ta-yoo-shcheekh oo-da-LYON-na, BY-la PREE-nya-ta ree-SHYE-nee-ye a ree-ar-ga-nee-ZA-tsee at-DYE-la.) — 'In connection with the increase in the number of employees working remotely, a decision was taken to reorganise the department' — expand it: В связи с тем, что число сотрудников, которые работают удалённо, увеличилось, решили реорганизовать отдел. (v SVYA-zee s tyem, shto chis-LO so-TROOD-nee-kaf, ka-TO-ry-ye ra-BO-ta-yut oo-da-LYON-na, oo-vee-LEE-chee-las, ree-SHEE-lee ree-ar-ga-nee-zo-VAT at-DYE-el.) — literally 'Because the number of employees who work remotely increased, they decided to reorganise the department'. Every word of the written sentence is now a word you could say aloud.
lessons.question: You must turn the written sentence Строительство нового моста было завершено досрочно into a spoken register without changing the content. What is the most characteristic single change?
lessons.answer: Replace the verbal noun and the short participle with a finite verb clause: Мост построили досрочно — 'they finished the bridge ahead of time'.
lessons.distractor: Replace было завершено with будет завершено, because spoken Russian prefers the future.
lessons.correction: Tense is not what distinguishes the registers; the spoken version may keep any tense. What distinguishes them is the nominalisation-plus-participle package. Строительство is a verbal noun that absorbs the verb 'to build' and carries no tense, and завершено is a short past passive participle that supplies the result with a neuter singular form because there is no Nominative subject. Spoken Russian undoes exactly that package: it puts a finite verb, here the third-plural построили, in place of both, and it names the bridge as the object or the subject. The third-plural form is the conversational way of saying 'someone did it' without naming anyone, which is why it sounds natural where the short participle sounds like a report.

depth.definitions: Register: a variety of language used for a particular purpose or communicative situation. Bookish written style (книжный стиль): the register of reports, laws, academic prose and news analysis. Conversational style (разговорный стиль): the register of speech. Participle: a verb form declined like an adjective. Verbal noun (отглагольное существительное): a noun built from a verb which names the event but carries no tense or person. Short form of a participle: the predicative, non-declining-by-gender form used in true passive sentences. который (ka-TO-ryy): the relative word which, used to build the spoken counterpart of a participle. Formulaic frame: a fixed written phrase such as в соответствии с or в связи с. Prerequisite: participles and gerunds from lessons 71 to 73, verbal nouns introduced here, reported speech from lesson 76.
depth.mechanism: The two registers are not random alternatives; they are two strategies for managing the same information, and each has a cost. The written strategy buys density and impersonal authority. By turning verbs into nouns and putting state into participles, a writer removes person, tense and agency from the sentence — exactly what a regulation, a report or a scientific description wants. The cost is that the reader must reconstruct all three, because agency and time are genuinely absent from the surface, not merely hidden. The spoken strategy buys recoverability: finite verbs force a subject, aspect forces a viewpoint, and the который-clause keeps each clause short enough to hold in working memory. Its cost is length. This trade explains the direction of the transformation in both directions: written to spoken means adding finite verbs and clauses; spoken to written means finding a noun for the event and a participle for the state. The mechanism has limits. Cornell notes that two deverbals do leak into speech — the short form of past passive participles and present deverbal adverbs — so the boundary is a strong tendency along a scale, not a wall. Idioms and bureaucratic formulas cannot be expanded freely either: продаётся (lesson 83) sits between the two, and Cornell's own advice is not to invent passive -ся forms because they often carry a bookish or bureaucratic flavour.
depth.secondExample: Take an instruction and move it the other way, from spoken to written. Spoken: Мы проверили документы и заметили, что в двух договорах нет подписи. (my pra-VYE-ree-lee da-koo-MYEN-ty ee za-MYE-tee-lee, shto v DVOOKH da-ga-VO-rakh nyet POD-pee-see.) — 'We checked the documents and noticed that two contracts lack a signature.' Written: При проверке документов было установлено отсутствие подписей в двух договорах. (pree pra-VYER-kye da-koo-MYEN-taf BY-la oos-ta-NOV-lye-na at-SOOT-stvee-ye PAD-pee-syey v DVOOKH da-ga-VO-rakh.) — 'On checking the documents, the absence of signatures in two contracts was established.' Notice what has been lost: the first person мы, the perfective verbs проверили and заметили, and the negation nyet, which has become the abstract noun отсутствие (at-SOOT-stvee-ye, absence). Notice what has been gained: a single subjectless frame proverka... ustanovleno that allows the writer to report a finding without saying who found it. A learner who can perform this transformation in both directions can also read both registers without translating the written one into bureaucratic English.
depth.mistake: The standard misconception is that written Russian is simply more polite or more advanced, so a learner imitates it in speech and sounds like a form read aloud. The diagnostic is easy: if your spoken Russian contains a short passive participle, a verbal noun in -ание/-ение, or a frame like в соответствии с and you are describing your own day, you have crossed registers. The second misconception is the reverse and is more damaging for reading: that a written sentence with no visible subject has no subject at all, so that было установлено is read as 'it was established' and left at that. There is always a recoverable agent or an intentional absence of one; deciding which is the interpretive work. The third error is to assume formality equals politeness. В связи с and вышеуказанный are formal but not polite; politeness in Russian has its own devices, which lesson 87 covers.
depth.application: Task: take the sentence В связи с увеличением числа сотрудников, работающих удалённо, было принято решение о реорганизации отдела and produce (a) a spoken-register paraphrase of at most fifteen words, and (b) a list of every grammatical change you made, labelled lexical, morphological or syntactic. Model response: 'В связи с тем, что всё больше сотрудников работают удалённо, решили реорганизовать отдел.' Changes: morphological — увеличение (verbal noun) becomes the comparative всё больше plus the finite verb работают; syntactic — the participial phrase работающих удалённо becomes a который-less relative clause with a finite verb; lexical — принято решение becomes решили; syntactic — the single sentence splits into two clauses linked by в связи с тем, что. Self-review rubric: (1) is every change labelled with the correct category? (2) does the paraphrase contain no short participle and no verbal noun? (3) if you reversed the task on your own sentence, would you recover the original content? Two of three yes answers is an acceptable first pass; repeat with a sentence from a Russian news report.
depth.summary: Register in Russian is carried by grammar, not only by vocabulary, and the load-bearing switch is the participle or verbal noun on the written side against a finite verb or который-clause on the spoken side. Learn the transformation in both directions and you gain two abilities at once: you can expand written prose into something you can say, and you can compress speech into something you can write. The limit to keep in mind is that the boundary is a tendency with known leaks, and that formality is not politeness. The next lesson takes the passive and impersonal constructions that this register depends on and makes them readable in their own right.

steps: Marker 1 — Event as noun vs event as verb. Written: строительство, увеличение, проверка. Spoken: строят, увеличилось, проверили. Reading reflex: find the missing verb and its subject before translating.

Marker 2 — Participle vs который-clause. Written: работающих удалённо, полученном письме. Spoken: которые работают удалённо, письмо, которое мы получили. Reading reflex: expand the participle, then read the expanded clause.

Marker 3 — Short passive participle vs third-plural verb. Written: было принято, было установлено. Spoken: приняли, установили, решили. Reading reflex: ask who acted; if nobody is named, note that the absence is deliberate.

Marker 4 — Written frame vs plain preposition. Written: в соответствии с решением, в связи с, вышеуказанный. Spoken: по решению, потому что, этот. Reading reflex: substitute the plain word before translating the clause.

Marker 5 — Attribution vs speech hedge. Written: согласно отчёту, по данным. Spoken: говорят, наверное, кажется. Reading reflex: both remove the writer's commitment, so record the source or the hedge rather than absorbing it into the claim.

lessons.title: Impersonal and passive constructions: reading sentences with no Nominative subject
lessons.explanation: Written Russian constantly uses sentences in which the person or thing you would expect to be the subject is not in the nominative at all. Cornell's sentence-type material names three kinds of predicate — verbs proper, short adjectives and predicatives including o-forms — and then states that 'there are many major sentence types that do not consist of the familiar Nominative subject plus verb predicate'. Three of those types carry most of the reading load. First, predicative sentences. 'Many sentences built around predicatives have elements that correspond to Nominative subjects in English, but which are not Nominative subjects in Russian.' Cornell's own examples: the English nominative we in 'We don't have any caviar' corresponds to the prepositional phrase u nas in У нас нет икры, and the English nominative I in 'I am cold' corresponds to the dative in Мне холодно. Because there is no nominative subject, past and future are expressed by the neuter singular forms of быть: 'Since there is no Nominative subject in the sentence, the neuter singular forms are used: было, будет.' So У нас нет икры becomes У нас не было икры and Икры не будет. Second, the pseudo-passive: an object-plus-verb-plus-subject order in which the nominative subject is saved until the end because Russian puts new information last. Cornell's example: the answer to Кто представил Сашу? is Сашу представила Маша — 'Sasha was introduced by Masha.' Third, the third-plural passive: a third person plural verb with no nominative subject at all. Cornell lists examples such as Студентам дадут по яблоку, and glosses говорят as 'it is said, one says, they say'. Russian also has a genuine passive, and it is worth knowing exactly where it sits: 'The true passive in Russian is formed by using the short form of the past passive participle.' So Эта статья написана Петром Ильичом — 'This article was written by Peter Ilyich' — with the agent in the instrumental (which you met in lesson 64) and the participle in a short form that agrees in gender and number but not case. The three constructions are not interchangeable, and Cornell gives the test that separates two of them: 'The difference between the 3rd plural passive and the past passive participle is that the 3rd plural implies that some human agency is responsible for the action, whereas the past passive participle has no such implication.' Practically: Магнитофон сломали implies a person deliberately broke the tape recorder, while Магнитофон сломан merely states the state it is in. Reading with this distinction available stops you from inventing agents that the Russian does not have and from missing agents that it does. The grammatical vocabulary is worth fixing here: безличное предложение (bees-LEECH-na-ye pred-la-ZHE-nee-ye) is an impersonal sentence, страдательный (stra-DA-tyel-nyy) means passive, and краткая форма (KRAT-ka-ya FOR-ma) is the short form of a participle or an adjective. Two forms from the example recur constantly in Russian administrative prose: построен (pa-STRO-yen), built, and сообщается (sa-ap-SHCHA-yet-sya), it is reported, the second being the impersonal frame that carries most official announcements.
lessons.example: Read one short report-like paragraph and classify every predicate. В прошлом году в городе был отремонтирован старый мост. Работы велись всё лето, и движение по мосту не закрывали. Теперь на мосту стоят новые фонари. Об этом много писали в газетах, но точной стоимости работ не сообщили. (v PROSH-lam ga-DOO v GO-ra-dye byl at-ree-man-TEE-ra-van STA-ryy most. ra-BO-ty vye-LEES fsyo LYE-ta, ee dvee-ZHE-nee-ye pa mos-TOO nye zak-ry-VA-lee. tee-PYER na mos-TOO sta-YAT NO-vy-ye fa-na-REE. ab EH-tam MNO-ga pee-SA-lee v ga-ZYE-takh, no TOCH-nay STO-ee-mas-tee ra-BOT nye sa-ap-SHCHEE-lee.) — 'Last year the old bridge in the town was repaired. The work went on all summer, and traffic on the bridge was not closed. Now there are new lamps on the bridge. The newspapers wrote about this a great deal, but the exact cost of the work was not reported.' Four different devices, one paragraph. Statement one is the true passive: был отремонтирован (byl at-ree-man-TEE-ra-van) is a short past passive participle, masculine singular to agree with мост, with the auxiliary был carrying the past tense. No person is implied — the sentence is about the bridge's condition, and a reader who inserts 'by someone' is adding something. Statement two uses the plural verb велись followed by не закрывали. не закрывали is a third-plural form: it means 'they did not close it', and because the third plural implies human agency, you are entitled to understand a nameless authority as the actor. Statement three is not passive at all: стоят (sta-YAT) is a position verb from lesson 68, and the sentence is an existence statement. Statement four uses wrote about it in the third plural (писали) and was not reported (не сообщили) likewise — both actionable, both deliberately agentless. Now run the reverse test. Suppose the last sentence had read точная стоимость работ не была сообщена. (TOCH-na-ya STO-ee-mast ra-BOT nye by-LA sa-ap-SHCHYE-na.) The short participle would state the fact as a condition and drop the human agency the third plural carries. The choice between these two is a real editorial decision, not a synonym preference. Note also the case-marking trap in the passive: the agent, if named, goes into the instrumental, so отремонтирован рабочими means 'repaired by the workers', while the object promoted to subject goes into the nominative.
lessons.question: A Russian news sentence reads Точная стоимость работ не сообщена. A learner translates it 'The exact cost of the work was not reported by anyone.' What is wrong with that translation?
lessons.answer: 'By anyone' is an invented agent. The short past passive participle states a condition and, unlike the third-plural form, carries no implication of human agency.
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, except that сообщена should be сообщено because the sentence has no subject.
lessons.correction: The participle agrees with стоимость, which is feminine singular, so сообщена is correct; the neuter form would be needed only if there were no nominative subject, as in the было/будет type. The real error is the added agent. Cornell states the distinction directly: the third plural implies that some human agency is responsible for the action, whereas the past passive participle has no such implication. If the writer had wanted to imply that some office failed to report the figure, не сообщили would have done it. With the short participle, the sentence reports the state of the information, and 'by anyone' imports an accusation that is not in the Russian.

depth.definitions: Nominative subject: the case in which the doer normally appears. Predicative: a word like холодно, нужно, нельзя, пора that can form a whole predicate with no nominative subject. The o-form is the predicative built on an adverb, for example холодно from холодный. Pseudo-passive: object plus verb plus nominative subject, used when the subject is new information. Third-plural passive: a third person plural verb with no nominative subject, implying unspecified human agency. True passive: быть or a short-form auxiliary plus the short form of a past passive participle, with any agent in the instrumental. Short form: the predicative, gender-and-number-agreeing form of a participle. Agreement: the requirement that a modifier match its noun in gender, number and case — participles changed into short forms agree in gender and number only. Prerequisite: dative predicatives and нужно from lessons 62 and 69; instrumental of agent from lesson 64; participles and gerunds from lessons 71 to 73.
depth.mechanism: The reason Russian can drop a nominative subject is that the nominative is not the only way to mark the most prominent participant in a clause. Case marks role, and word order marks information structure; the nominative subject is then only one of several possible arrangements, not a structural necessity as it is in English. Three consequences follow for a reader. First, the form of the verb no longer tells you who is doing anything, so you must read case marking to find the participant and agreement to find the gender and number of whatever the participle controls. Second, the choice among the agentless options is informative because each one carries a different amount of agency: the third plural implies persons, the short participle implies none, and the -ся passive such as продаётся sits between them and often sounds bureaucratic, which is why Cornell advises against inventing new ones. Third, tense has to be carried by something external — the neuter singular было and будет in the predicative type, the auxiliary был/была/было/были in the true passive — so a sentence with no auxiliary and no tense inflection is tenseless by design and reads as a general statement. The limits are worth stating: the third-plural passive is genuinely ambiguous between 'they' and 'people in general', and no amount of grammar resolves that; only context does. And a short participle can be stative rather than passive, as in Магазин закрыт, which describes a state and does not require a reading of an event at all.
depth.secondExample: Compare three ways to say that the library was closed, and watch the amount of implied agency change. (1) Библиотека закрыта. (beeb-lee-a-TYE-ka zak-RY-ta.) — short participle, feminine. The sentence describes the library's present condition. Nobody is implied; this is the sentence you would meet on a notice. (2) Библиотеку закрыли. (beeb-lee-a-TYE-koo zak-RY-lee.) — accusative object plus third plural. The library was closed, and unnamed people did it. This is what you say when you know there was a decision. (3) Библиотека была закрыта в прошлом году. (beeb-lee-a-TYE-ka by-LA zak-RY-ta v PROSH-lam ga-DOO.) — the same short participle with the auxiliary, which supplies past tense and reads as an event report. Now the reading question becomes answerable: sentence (1) tells you the state, sentence (2) tells you that a person acted, sentence (3) tells you when the action is dated. This three-way contrast is the single most useful framework for reading Russian news and notices, and it is precisely the distinction that a learner who translates everything as 'was closed' will never see.
depth.mistake: The most frequent error is to translate every agentless-looking sentence with an English passive and to accept whatever agent the passive suggests. That turns Магнитофон сломан ('the tape recorder is broken', a state) into 'someone broke the tape recorder', and it turns точная стоимость не сообщена into an accusation. The diagnostic is to ask whether the construction licenses an agent: third plural yes, short participle no, -ся passive only weakly. The second error is a grammatical one with a clear test: learners want to force a nominative subject onto Mne kholodno, producing something like *Я холодный, which is a different and wrong statement about a person's temperament. In the predicative type the dative participant is the person affected, and it never becomes nominative. The third error is to read было/будет in the predicative type as 'it was' with a hidden subject; because there is no nominative subject those forms are frozen in the neuter singular, so было холодно cannot become *были холодно.
depth.application: Task: take four sentences — Мост отремонтировали; Мост был отремонтирован; Мост отремонтирован; Мост ремонтируется — and for each write (a) a literal English gloss, (b) the amount of agency you are entitled to read, and (c) one situation in which a Russian writer would choose it. Model response, for Мост отремонтировали: 'They repaired the bridge'; agency — unnamed persons who acted; chosen in a news item where a decision-maker exists but is irrelevant. For Мост был отремонтирован: 'The bridge was repaired' as an event; agency — none implied; chosen in a formal report. For Мост отремонтирован: 'The bridge is repaired / in a repaired state'; agency — none; chosen on a sign or in a condition report. For Мост ремонтируется: 'The bridge is being repaired / is under repair'; agency — weak, and the form is bookish; chosen in a bureaucratic notice. Self-review rubric: (1) does each gloss keep the correct tense? (2) is the agency claim defensible from the form alone? (3) could a Russian writer have used the sentence you chose instead? Two of three yes answers passes.
depth.summary: Russian builds whole sentences without a nominative subject, and the reader's job is to locate the participant by case, locate the tense in an auxiliary or a frozen neuter form, and decide how much agency the construction licenses. The three-way contrast between the third plural, the true passive with a short participle, and the pseudo-passive is the framework that makes written Russian tractable, and Cornell's agency test is the single most useful sentence in the material. Keep the limits in view: the third plural is genuinely ambiguous, the -ся passive is bookish and not freely productive, and short participles are often stative rather than passive. Lesson 84 now takes the other half of written density, the verbal noun, and shows how it compresses a clause into a single word.

visual.title: Agentless-sentence decision ladder: four constructions, four agency readings
visual.description: A labelled decision sequence that takes an agentless Russian sentence and routes it to one of four constructions, each with its own licensed agency reading and its own register. Text steps, not video.
steps: Step 1 — Is there a nominative noun agreeing with the predicate? If no, the sentence is one of the subjectless types; go to Step 2. If yes, it is an ordinary subject-plus-predicate sentence and this ladder does not apply.

Step 2 — Is the predicate a predicative word (холодно, нужно, нельзя, пора, ясно) or a frozen neuter было/будет plus one? If yes, this is a predicative sentence: the affected person is in the dative or in у plus genitive, and there is no subject to look for.
Step 3 — Is the verb third person plural? If yes, this is the third-plural passive: read in unnamed human agents, and expect a colloquial or news register.

Step 4 — Is there a short participle with an auxiliary (был, была, было, были, будет) or with a present-tense zero? If yes, this is the true passive: read no agent at all, and check whether the sense is an event or a state.

Step 5 — Does the verb end in -ся and name a bookish process (продаётся, ремонтируется)? If yes, read it as a bureaucratic middle: an agent is weakly available but the writer is avoiding one. Do not invent new -ся passives when speaking.

lessons.title: Verbal nouns and how they compress a clause into a word
lessons.explanation: The verbal noun is the single largest source of difficulty in reading Russian non-fiction, and it is also the most mechanical to solve, because it has a small number of partly reliable diagnostics. Cornell introduces the problem with a warning about appearance: 'Nouns derived from verbs (deverbal nouns) look deceptively like past passive participles.' The classic pair is открытие (at-KRY-tee-ye, a discovery) against открытый (at-KRY-tyy, opened), and предложение (pred-la-ZHE-nee-ye, a proposal or a sentence) against предложенный (pred-LO-zhen-nyy, proposed). Cornell then gives three tests, and they are worth memorising as a checklist. One, endings: 'The nouns are all neuter'; предложения-ми is an instrumental plural noun while предложенн-ыми is an instrumental plural past passive participle, so the case ending itself tells you the part of speech. Two, the vowel: 'Nouns have -и- after the -т- or -н-; past passive participles do not' — the noun stem ends in a vowel, the participial stem in a consonant, as in предложени-е against предложенн-ый. Three, the doubled consonant: 'The noun suffix has a single -н-, but the long participial suffix has double -нн-.' Apply the three in order and most ambiguous forms resolve. What a verbal noun does to a sentence is compress it. A clause such as Мы обсудили проект (my ab-soo-DEE-lee pra-YEKT, 'we discussed the project') becomes обсуждение проекта (ab-soozh-DYE-nee-ye pra-YEK-ta, 'the discussion of the project'). The subject disappears; the tense disappears; the verb becomes a noun that takes a genitive complement where the verb took a direct object. That is the trade: the writer gains a compact noun that can be the subject, the object or the object of a preposition of another sentence, and the reader loses person and time. Linguistics describes the general phenomenon in neutral terms: nominalization covers nouns formed from other types of words, and the term verbal noun is used for a noun that is formed from a verb or otherwise corresponds to one. English does the same thing with the -ing and -tion suffixes, which is why the English gloss 'the discussion of the project' is often the natural translation. The reading strategy is therefore double translation. Translate the verbal noun first as a noun in English, then re-expand it into a clause and see whether that clause fits the sentence. При обсуждении проекта мы решили изменить сроки (pree ab-soozh-DYE-nee-ee pra-YEK-ta my ree-SHEE-lee eez-mee-NEET SRO-kee) — 'During the discussion of the project we decided to change the deadlines' — expands cleanly to Когда мы обсуждали проект, мы решили изменить сроки (kag-DA my ab-soozh-DA-lee pra-YEKT, my ree-SHEE-lee eez-mee-NEET SRO-kee), 'When we were discussing the project, we decided to change the deadlines.' The expansion supplies a subject, a tense and an aspect, and often makes the sentence readable for the first time. Three frequent verbal nouns are worth having ready before you read anything official: строительство (stra-EE-tyel-stva), construction or building work, развитие (raz-VEE-tee-ye), development, and применение (pree-mee-NYE-nee-ye), application or use.
lessons.example: Here is a paragraph written in the register verbal nouns produce, followed by the same content unpacked. Written: После завершения ремонта началось обсуждение планов расширения производства. Увеличение числа заказов потребовало проверки оборудования. Отсутствие свободных помещений затрудняет выполнение заказов. (POS-lye za-veer-SHYE-nee-ya ree-MON-ta na-cha-LOS ab-soozh-DYE-nee-ye PLA-naf ras-shee-RYE-nee-ya pra-eez-VOT-stva. oo-vee-LEE-chee-nee-ye chis-LA za-KA-zaf pa-tryE-ba-va-la pra-VYER-kee a-ba-ROO-da-va-nee-ya. at-SOOT-stvee-ye sva-BOD-nykh pa-mye-SHCHE-nee an at-trood-NYA-yet vyp-al-NYE-nee-ye za-KA-zaf.) — 'After the completion of the repair, discussion of plans for the expansion of production began. The increase in the number of orders required a check of the equipment. The absence of free premises makes the fulfilment of orders difficult.' Count the verbal nouns: завершение, обсуждение, расширение, увеличение, проверка, отсутствие, выполнение. Seven nouns, no person, and only four finite verbs in the whole paragraph — началось, потребовало, затрудняет, plus the infinitive-free remainder. Now unpack it clause by clause. После завершения ремонта = after they had finished the repair; обсуждение планов расширения производства = they discussed plans to expand production, where два genitives stack, планов and расширения, and the second modifies the first; проверка оборудования = someone checked the equipment; отсутствие свободных помещений = there are no free premises, where the abstract noun отсутствие has replaced the negated verb нет. Unpacked: Когда ремонт закончился, начали обсуждать планы расширения производства. Заказов стало больше, поэтому пришлось проверить оборудование. Свободных помещений нет, поэтому выполнять заказы труднее. (kag-DA ree-MONT za-KON-cheel-sya, NA-cha-lee ab-soozh-DAT PLA-ny ras-shee-RYE-nee-ya pra-eez-VOT-stva. za-KA-zaf STA-la BOL-she, pa-EH-ta-moo pree-shLOS pra-VYE-reet a-ba-ROO-da-va-nee-ye. sva-BOD-nykh pa-mye-SHCHE-nee nyet, pa-EH-ta-moo vyp-al-NYAT za-KA-zy trood-NYE-ye.) — 'When the repair finished, they began to discuss plans for expanding production. There were more orders, so the equipment had to be checked. There are no free premises, so fulfilling orders is harder.' The unpacked version is roughly twice as long and is sayable aloud. Notice that the genitive stacking survives the unpacking in планы расширения производства; only the clause markers change.
lessons.question: A learner meets the form обсуждения in the instrumental plural position within a sentence and reads it as a participle meaning 'discussing'. Which diagnostic settles the question fastest?
lessons.answer: Both the ending and the stem: the noun is neuter with a case ending of its own, and its stem keeps -и- after -н- with a single -н-, whereas the participle has double -нн- and consonant-final participial endings.
lessons.distractor: The meaning settles it: обсуждения cannot be a participle because Russian has no participle from обсуждать.
lessons.correction: обсуждать does have a participle, обсуждаемый (ab-soozh-DA-ye-myy, 'being discussed'), so the appeal to a gap in the paradigm is simply false. Meaning is also the wrong tool because the whole difficulty is that the two forms look alike and are translated differently before you know which one you have. Cornell gives three form-level diagnostics and the two quoted here are decisive: nouns are neuter with noun endings and have -и- after -т- or -н- because the noun stem is vowel-final, while long participles have double -нн- and take adjective endings. Use the forms first, then interpret.

depth.definitions: Verbal noun (отглагольное существительное): a noun formed from a verb or otherwise corresponding to it, naming an event or a result rather than asserting one. Nominalization: the grammatical formation of nouns from other types of words. Genitive complement: the case a verbal noun uses where the corresponding verb used a direct object — обсуждение проекта against обсуждать проект. Long form of a participle: the adjective-like form with double -нн- for the -нн- type. Short form: the predicative form used in true passives, which cannot take the noun's vowel-final stem. Stacked genitives: two or more genitives in a row, each modifying the one before. Prerequisite: past passive participles from lesson 71, participles versus который-clauses from lesson 73, and the register split from lesson 82.
depth.mechanism: A verbal noun works by moving an event out of the verb slot and into a noun slot, and this has three mechanical consequences. First, the event loses person and tense, because the noun paradigm has neither; a verbal noun cannot be past or future on its own, so any time reference has to come from a prepositional phrase, from the surrounding sentence or from the reader's knowledge. That is why written business prose is so often vague about when things happened. Second, the noun takes noun syntax: the direct object of the verb becomes a genitive complement, and adverbial modifiers become adjectives, so проверять оборудование тщательно becomes тщательная проверка оборудования. Third, verbal nouns are productive in the -ание/-ение and -тие classes and in the zero-suffix class (проверка, ремонт, отказ), which is precisely why they collide in form with participles in the -ние class. Cornell's three tests exploit the collision: the noun is neuter, its stem is vowel-final, and it has one -н-. Be aware of the limits. Not every verbal noun corresponds to a verb you know, and some have drifted semantically: открытие is both 'a discovery' and 'an opening', and предложение is both 'a proposal' and 'a sentence'. The expansion strategy also has a hard limit: it cannot recover a subject that the writer genuinely did not have in mind, so 'проверка оборудования' may have to stay subjectless in your translation just as it is in the Russian.
depth.secondExample: Take a single verb and watch it travel across the registers, then across parts of speech. Verb, spoken: Мы проверили документы. (my pra-VYE-ree-lee da-koo-MYEN-ty.) — 'We checked the documents.' Participle, written: проверенные документы (pra-VYE-ryen-ny-ye da-koo-MYEN-ty) — 'the checked documents', where проверенный has double -нн- and adjective endings. Gerund, written: Проверив документы, мы подписали договор. (pra-VYE-reef da-koo-MYEN-ty, my pad-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR.) — 'Having checked the documents, we signed the contract', from lesson 72. Verbal noun, written: После проверки документов мы подписали договор. (POS-lye pra-VYER-kee da-koo-MYEN-taf my pad-pee-SA-lee da-ga-VOR.) — 'After checking the documents, we signed the contract.' Four forms, one event. Now look for the diagnostic in each: the participle has -нн- and adjective endings; the gerund is indeclinable and ends in -в; the verbal noun has noun endings and takes a genitive complement. This is the same set of decisions you make when reading a contract, a report or a news analysis, and it is why lesson 71 introduced the six deverbal forms as a chart rather than as separate topics.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error is to read a verbal noun as a participle and therefore build a wrong clause around it. A learner translating После проверки оборудования начался ремонт as 'After the equipment checked, the repair began' has taken the noun проверки for a verb form and made the equipment the subject. The diagnostic is the three-test checklist in order: neuter gender, vowel-final stem with -и- after -т- or -н-, single -н-. A second error is to treat a verbal noun as if it carried the tense of the sentence: in Отсутствие свободных помещений затрудняет выполнение заказов the noun отсутствие has no temporal value at all, and translating it as 'the absence has been' invents a perfect. A third error is to flatten genitive stacks. In обсуждение планов расширения производства the correct English is 'discussion of plans for expanding production'; reading it as 'discussion of the expanding of production plans' gets the syntactic relations backwards.
depth.application: Task: take the written sentence Увеличение числа заказов потребовало проверки оборудования и обсуждения планов расширения производства. Produce (a) a list of every verbal noun with its governing verb, (b) an unpacked spoken-register version, and (c) a note on what information the written version does not state. Model response: (a) увеличение from увеличиться, проверка from проверять, обсуждение from обсуждать, расширение from расширять; (b) Because the number of orders increased, they had to check the equipment and discuss plans to expand production; (c) the written version does not say who checked or discussed anything and does not date the check, and the expansion is named as a plan rather than as an action. Self-review rubric: (1) does every verbal noun in your list resolve to a verb you can name? (2) does your unpacked version contain a finite verb for every noun you removed? (3) have you correctly named what is absent — person, tense, or both? Two of three yes answers is a working pass; redo it on a paragraph from a Russian annual report.
depth.summary: Verbal nouns are the density engine of written Russian. They convert events into things, which lets a writer stack them as subjects and genitive complements, and the price is the loss of person and tense. Cornell's three form tests — neuter noun endings, -и- after -т- or -н-, single -н- against the participle's -нн- — resolve the collision with past passive participles, and the double-translation strategy (noun first, then re-expand into a clause) restores readability. Limits to respect: some verbs have no verbal noun you know, some nouns have drifted semantically, and expansion cannot supply an agent the writer never had in mind. This lesson closes the first unit, in which you built the reading apparatus: argument structure, register, subjectless sentences and compressed clauses. The second unit turns that apparatus toward production.

lessons.title: Aspect in narrative versus aspect in instruction
lessons.explanation: Lesson 79 showed the division of labour inside a story: the perfective carries the chain of bounded events, and the imperfective carries the setting, the habits and the simultaneous background. That framework transfers to instruction, but the balance inverts, and understanding why is the whole lesson. Cornell states the basic contrast as a pair of uses: 'Use the Perfective partner to talk about the specific instance; use the Imperfective partner to talk about doing the same thing in general, e.g. as a matter of habit or principle.' An instruction is, by default, a sequence of specific instances: you want each step performed once and finished before the next. That is why procedural Russian is dense with perfective imperatives — нарежьте (na-RYEZH-tye, cut up), добавьте (da-BAV-tye, add), включите (vlyoo-CHEE-tye, switch on), проверьте (pra-VYER-tye, check). But Russian has a second imperative aspect with a different job, and Cornell describes it precisely in the context of hospitality: 'To add a tone of politeness and friendliness in a host-guest situation, the Imperfective aspect of Imperatives is used instead of the Perfective', because 'you are merely telling him to start doing it', whereas 'A Perfective verb suggests that you want it completed.' Cornell's example pair is Садитесь ('have a seat', imperfective) against Сядьте ('sit down', perfective), and its doctor-versus-host diagnosis is the key: the host says Снимайте пальто, садитесь, while a doctor giving instructions says Снимите рубашку и сядьте на стол — 'because he is giving you specific directions that he wants you to follow to the end.' Procedures use that same imperfective in a third way: for actions that are meant to be repeated or continued. Помешивайте (pa-MYE-shee-vay-tye, keep stirring) and добавляйте понемногу (da-bav-LYAY-tye pa-nee-MNO-goo, add a little at a time) describe an activity held open, not a bounded step. And negation in instructions follows the tendency you already know from lesson 79: the imperfective is the natural negative, so Не открывайте окно (nye at-kry-VAY-tye ak-NO, don't open the window) means exactly that as a standing instruction, and it does not mean 'you tried to open it and failed'. The reading consequence is a test you can apply to any set of steps. Ask of each imperative: is this one bounded completion, an activity to keep going, or a standing prohibition? Perfective, imperfective with an iterative sense, and imperfective under negation respectively. Cornell also gives the statistical caveat you must keep in mind from the aspect-and-plurality material: 'There is an affinity between Imperfective aspect and plural objects', and this 'is somewhat vague; it is a statistical fact rather than a grammatical rule.' Instructions that handle many objects at once therefore drift imperfective for statistical rather than grammatical reasons. Fix the register vocabulary as well: an инструкция (een-STROOK-tsee-ya) is a set of instructions, a процедура (pra-tsee-DOO-ra) is a procedure, and a рецепт (ree-TSEPT) is a recipe or a prescription. One completion phrase returns constantly in cooking instructions, довести до кипения (da-vees-TEE da kee-PYE-nee-ya), to bring to the boil, and it is perfective precisely because the bringing is a bounded act.
lessons.example: Compare a recipe written in the procedural register with the same events retold as a narrative. Procedure: Нарежьте лук, добавьте его к мясу и обжарьте пять минут. Затем добавьте воду и варите на маленьком огне. Помешивайте каждые пять минут. Не открывайте крышку. (na-RYEZH-tye look, da-BAV-tye ee-VO k MYA-soo ee ab-ZHAR-tye pyat mee-NOOT. za-TYEM da-BAV-tye va-DOO ee va-REE-tye na MA-lyen-kam ag-NYE. pa-MYE-shee-vay-tye KAZH-dy-ye pyat mee-NOOT. nye at-kry-VAY-tye KRYSH-koo.) — 'Cut up the onion, add it to the meat and fry for five minutes. Then add water and cook on a low heat. Stir every five minutes. Do not open the lid.' Narrative retelling of the same cooking: Вчера я готовила суп. Я нарезала лук, добавила его к мясу и обжарила пять минут. Потом я добавила воду и варила суп на маленьком огне. Я помешивала каждые пять минут и не открывала крышку. (fchee-RA ya ga-TO-vee-la soop. ya na-RYE-za-la look, da-BA-vee-la ee-VO k MYA-soo ee ab-ZHA-ree-la pyat mee-NOOT. pa-TOM ya da-BA-vee-la va-DOO ee va-REE-la soop na MA-lyen-kam ag-NYE. ya pa-MYE-shee-va-la KAZH-dy-ye pyat mee-NOOT ee nye at-kry-VA-la KRYSH-koo.) — 'Yesterday I made soup. I cut up the onion, added it to the meat and fried it for five minutes. Then I added the water and cooked the soup on a low heat. I stirred every five minutes and did not open the lid.' Now compare aspect by aspect. The bounded steps match: нарежьте/нарезала, добавьте/добавила, обжарьте/обжарила are perfective in both. The difference appears exactly where the two registers ask different questions. The procedure says варите (implicitly imperfective for a sustained process) where the narrative also says варила (imperfective, because it lasted); but the procedure could have said сварите if it meant 'bring it to completion', and a reader who translates варите as 'you will have cooked it' has added a boundary that is not there. The procedure's помешивайте (imperfective, iterative) corresponds to the narrative's помешивала (imperfective, repeated habit), so that pair is stable. And the prohibition Не открывайте крышку (imperfective) corresponds to не открывала (imperfective) — because what is being denied is any occurrence of the action, which is the negation tendency from lesson 79, not an attempt that failed. Finally, note that the procedure has no tense at all: tense is supplied entirely by the imperative form plus затем, and aspect is doing the whole job of distinguishing 'do this once', 'keep doing this' and 'never do this'.
lessons.question: A Russian manual writes Помешивайте каждые пять минут, and the same manual two lines earlier writes Добавьте соль. Why do the two imperatives have different aspects?
lessons.answer: Добавьте is perfective because it is a single bounded step to be completed once; помешивайте is imperfective because it names an activity to be kept going at intervals, which is the repeated-action use of the imperfective.
lessons.distractor: Добавьте is perfective because it is negated nowhere in the sentence, and помешивайте is imperfective because it is followed by a time expression.
lessons.correction: Neither explanation is right. Aspect is not governed by the presence or absence of negation — it is governed by whether the writer wants a boundary. Cornell's contrast is between the specific instance (perfective) and doing the same thing in general or as a matter of habit (imperfective), and каждые пять минут makes the stirring habitual and repeated, which is exactly the imperfective's territory; a time expression by itself does not force aspect, since Добавьте через пять минут is a perfectly ordinary perfective instruction with a time phrase. The real question to ask is whether the action is meant to be finished once or kept going, and in this pair the manual is asking for one completed act and then an ongoing activity.

depth.definitions: Aspect: the choice between viewing an action as a bounded whole and viewing it as an ongoing, repeated or unbounded process. Perfective: views the action as bounded, typically a single completed instance. Imperfective: views it without a boundary — in progress, repeated or habitual. Iterative: repeated, as in помешивайте, stir at intervals. Procedural register: the language of instructions, recipes and manuals, typically imperative and tenseless. Standing instruction: a rule that holds generally, naturally imperfective under negation. Aspect pair: two verbs, one perfective and one imperfective, sharing a lexical meaning, such as открыть and открывать. Prerequisite: the aspect material of lessons 56 and 79, imperatives from lessons 69 and 88, and the register distinction from lesson 82.
depth.mechanism: The inversion happens because narrative and instruction want different things from time. A narrative reports a sequence of events that have already happened and must be ordered, so the perfective does the reporting and the imperfective supplies the world in which the events occur. An instruction does not report anything; it asks for a future performance, and the only grammatical resource it has for distinguishing kinds of performance is aspect, because the imperative has no tense. That gives the imperfective two entirely separate jobs in instructions. The first is politeness: Cornell's host says садитесь rather than сядьте because merely saying 'start doing this' is less demanding than saying 'get this done'. The second is iterativity: помешивайте describes an activity held open, and this use is productive in recipes, exercise routines and maintenance manuals, precisely where an ongoing activity is the point. Negation supplies a third systematic use, since a standing prohibition naturally forbids the action as such. The limits matter. Cornell is explicit that the aspect-and-plurality affinity is statistical, not grammatical, so a plural object does not compel the imperfective. The polite-imperfective use is also idiomatic rather than fully productive: Cornell notes that the meaning of some verbs may preclude a polite imperative at all, giving Отстань от меня as perfective-only, and that a dog trainer's Сидеть! uses an infinitive for a stronger command than any imperative. Do not generalise the politeness reading to every imperfective imperative you meet in a manual, where the likely motive is iterativity.
depth.secondExample: Run the same comparison on a non-culinary procedure, where the aspect decisions are load-bearing rather than decorative. Instruction (a training manual): Перед началом работы проверьте оборудование. Включите питание и подождите две минуты. Нажмите кнопку проверки. Если появится сигнал, не продолжайте и позвоните мастеру. (PYE-ryet na-CHA-lam ra-BO-ty pra-VYER-tye a-ba-ROO-da-va-nee-ye. vlyoo-CHEE-tye pee-TA-nee-ye ee pa-dazh-DEE-tye dva MYE-noo-ty. nazh-MEE-tye KNOP-koo pra-VYER-kee. YES-lee pa-YA-veet-sya seeg-NAL, nye pra-dal-ZHAY-tye ee paz-va-NEE-tye MA-ste-roo.) — 'Before starting work, check the equipment. Switch on the power and wait two minutes. Press the check button. If a signal appears, do not go on, and phone the technician.' Every imperative here is perfective except the prohibition, which is imperfective, and the criterion is uniformly bounded completion: check, switch on, wait, press, phone. Narrative of the same shift: Утром я проверил оборудование, включил питание и подождал две минуты, а потом нажал кнопку. Сигнал не появился, поэтому я продолжал работу. (OO-tram ya pra-VYE-reel a-ba-ROO-da-va-nee-ye, vlyoo-CHEEL pee-TA-nee-ye ee pa-dazh-DAL dva mee-NOO-ty, a pa-TOM na-ZHAL KNOP-koo. seeg-NAL nye pa-ya-VEEL-sya, pa-EH-ta-moo ya pra-dal-ZHAL ra-BO-too.) — 'In the morning I checked the equipment, switched on the power and waited two minutes, then pressed the button. No signal appeared, so I continued working.' The perfective chain is identical; what changes is that the narrative supplies persons and past tense, and that продолжать appears in the imperfective because the continuing is what was in progress. Read both and ask which verbs could not be swapped between the two texts: the prohibition and the continuing are the two that cannot.
depth.mistake: The standard error is to assume one aspect belongs to instructions, usually the perfective, and to lose every distinction the aspect choice is carrying. A learner who reads Помешивайте as 'stir it (once)' will undercook the dish and mistranslate the manual; a learner who reads Не открывайте крышку as 'you failed to open the lid' has imported the wrong negation reading. The diagnostic question is always: does the writer want a boundary here? A second error is to over-apply the politeness reading. Cornell's hospitality examples are clichés of a particular situation; a recipe's imperfective is usually iterative, not polite, and reading politeness into a maintenance manual produces a translation that sounds absurd. The third error is the reverse of the first: learning that imperfective imperatives sound polite and then using them for safety-critical steps, which weakens the instruction exactly where strength is needed. Russian manuals use the perfective for steps that must be completed, and that is not an accident of style.
depth.application: Task: take a procedure you perform regularly and write it twice, once as a procedural text of four to six imperative steps and once as a narrative of your last performance of it. Then underline every aspect choice that differs between the two versions and explain each difference in one clause. Model response for making tea: procedure — Вскипятите воду. Насыпьте чай в чашку. Залейте его кипятком. Подождите три минуты. Не размешивайте сразу. (vskee-pee-TEE-tye va-DOO. na-SYP-tye chay v CHASH-koo. zay-LYE-tye ee-VO keep-it-KOM. pa-dazh-DEE-tye tree mee-NOO-ty. nye raz-MYE-shee-vay-tye SRA-zoo.) narrative — Вчера я вскипятила воду, насыпала чай, залила кипятком и подождала три минуты. Explanation of the only differing choice: не размешивайте is imperfective in both because it is a prohibition, which denies every occurrence of the action rather than one failed attempt. Self-review rubric: (1) is every step you intend to be completed once in the perfective? (2) does every iterative or sustaining instruction use the imperfective, and can you say why in one clause? (3) does your narrative use the imperative anywhere, which would be a register break? Three yes answers is a pass; otherwise revise the aspect choices, not the wording.
depth.summary: Aspect in narrative and aspect in instruction answer different questions. Narrative orders events, so the perfective reports and the imperfective backgrounds. Instruction requests future performances with no tense of its own, so the aspect must carry completion, continuation, iteration and prohibition. Three readings follow: perfective imperative means complete this step; imperfective imperative means keep doing this, or start doing this, with politeness as one idiomatic use; imperfective under negation means never do this. Keep the two caveats: the plural-object affinity is statistical, and the polite-imperative pattern is idiomatic and not freely productive. With this, Unit 1 is complete — you can read an argumentative paragraph, place it in a register, parse its subjectless and compressed sentences, and now distinguish procedure from narrative. Unit 2 turns to production: uncertainty, opinion, procedure out loud, summary and a sustained conversation.

visual.title: Aspect decision test for a step in a procedure: three questions, three aspects
visual.description: A labelled decision sequence that takes one step of a procedure and routes it to perfective, iterative imperfective or prohibitive imperfective, with the reading each produces. Text steps, not video.
steps: Step 1 — Is the step meant to be finished once before the next step begins? If yes, use the perfective imperative and read it as a bounded instruction. Example: Нарежьте лук. Translation: 'Cut up the onion', once, completely.

Step 2 — Is the step an activity to be kept going or repeated at intervals? If yes, use the imperfective imperative and read it as an open activity. Example: Помешивайте каждые пять минут. Translation: 'Keep stirring every five minutes'.

Step 3 — Is the step a prohibition that holds for the whole procedure? If yes, use the imperfective under negation and read it as a standing ban, not a failed attempt. Example: Не открывайте крышку. Translation: 'Do not open the lid', ever, during this procedure.

Step 4 — Is the step merely an invitation to begin? If yes, the imperfective may be a politeness choice rather than an iterative one. Example: Садитесь. Translation: 'Have a seat, please'. Do not carry this reading into a manual, where iterativity or prohibition is the likelier motive.

Step 5 — Switch registers. If you now retell the same steps as something that happened, expect the perfective chain to survive and expect person and past tense to be added. Example: Я нарезала лук, добавила его к мясу и варила суп на маленьком огне.
