questions.prompt: You are handed a Russian paragraph that begins with a factual sentence and then contains Однако, во-первых and поэтому. You have twenty minutes and one reading. What order of operations gives you the argument rather than a paraphrase of the wording?
questions.answer: Scan for the connective signals first and label each sentence as claim, support, concession or conclusion, then translate, then check who owns each part.
questions.distractor: Translate every sentence in sequence and identify the claim as the longest sentence in the paragraph.
questions.correction: Translating first produces a summary of the words, not of the argument, and length is unrelated to prominence: in the lesson's passage the conclusion is the shortest sentence. The signals are what mark the seams, and the attribution phrases are what tell you whose claim each part is. Reading order is therefore signal-scan, labelling, translation, ownership check.

questions.prompt: You have to say the content of the written sentence Строительство нового моста было завершено досрочно aloud, in conversation. Which version is the correct register flip?
questions.answer: Мост построили досрочно - the verbal noun and the short participle give way to one third-plural finite verb.
questions.distractor: Мост был завершён досрочно - drop the verbal noun and keep the short participle, since participles are grammatical in both registers.
questions.correction: Cornell notes that the short forms of past passive participles do occur in conversational style, but the sentence you would actually say still needs a finite verb rather than a nominalised statement of condition. Строительство absorbs the verb and carries no tense or person, and завершено states a result; spoken Russian replaces both with построили, which supplies a tense, a completed aspect and an unnamed human agent all at once.

questions.prompt: A paragraph contains Магнитофон сломан and two sentences later Магнитофон сломали. What is the reading difference between the two forms?
questions.answer: Сломан states a present condition with no agent implied; сломали implies unnamed people who acted.
questions.distractor: Сломан attributes the damage to a specific named repairer; сломали states a permanent property of the object.
questions.correction: Cornell states the distinction directly: the third-plural passive implies that some human agency is responsible for the action, whereas the past passive participle has no such implication. So the short participle is a state report and the third plural is an event with an unnamed actor. Neither form names anybody, and reading a named person into сломан adds information the Russian does not contain.

questions.prompt: You meet the form предложения in a sentence and cannot tell whether it is a verbal noun or a past passive participle. Which diagnostic settles it, and on what evidence?
questions.answer: Inspect the stem and ending: the noun is neuter with a single -н- and keeps -и- after -н-, while the participle has -нн- and adjective endings.
questions.distractor: Inspect the position: a form before a genitive noun is a participle, and a form after a preposition is a verbal noun.
questions.correction: Position is a weak cue and will mislead you, because verbal nouns take genitive complements and participles agree with the nouns they modify, so both can appear next to a noun. Cornell's three tests are form-level and reliable: nouns are neuter, the noun stem is vowel-final and shows -и- after -т- or -н-, and the noun suffix has one -н- against the participle's -нн-. Apply the tests, then interpret.

questions.prompt: A manual gives Помешивайте каждые пять минут where the previous step was Добавьте соль. Which statement correctly explains the two aspect choices?
questions.answer: Добавьте is perfective for one bounded step, and помешивайте is imperfective because the stirring is an activity to be kept going at intervals.
questions.distractor: Both are imperfective instructions, and длина is the only difference: the longer form is used for steps that take longer.
questions.correction: Добавьте is not imperfective - it is the perfective imperative of добавить, and its ви- form ends in -те. Cornell's contrast is between the specific bounded instance and doing something repeatedly or habitually, and каждые пять минут places the stirring squarely in the second category. Form length has no aspect value; the question to ask is always whether the writer wants a boundary here.

units.title: Producing Russian: uncertainty, opinion, procedure, summary and a sustained conversation

lessons.title: Uncertainty, inference and deduction: saying how you know and how sure you are
lessons.explanation: Russian separates two questions that English often blurs: how do you know, and how sure are you? Linguistics calls the first evidentiality and the second epistemic modality, and Russian has ready-made vocabulary for both. Evidentiality, in the standard formulation, is the indication of the nature of evidence for a given statement, that is, whether evidence exists for the statement and if so what kind, and the same source distinguishes direct evidentials, for information perceived by the speaker, from indirect ones such as quotatives and inferentials. Russian does not inflect for evidentiality as some languages do, which is why that source is careful to say that European languages often use modal verbs or other lexical means. Russian's lexical means are exactly the frame you are learning here: говорят (ga-va-RYAT, they say) for hearsay, судя по (soo-DYA pa, judging by) for inference from present evidence, по-видимому (pa-VEE-dee-ma-moo, apparently) and похоже (pa-KHO-zhe, it seems) for an inference you are not certain of, оказывается (a-KA-zy-va-yet-sya, it turns out) for a conclusion that arrived suddenly, and должно быть (dolzh-NO byt) for a deduction you are confident in. Cornell's material confirms how deeply hearsay is built into ordinary Russian syntax. Its third-plural passive page glosses говорят as it is said, one says, they say, and the sentence frame needs no subject at all: Говорят, что он хороший преподаватель (ga-va-RYAT, shto on ha-RO-shiy pree-pa-da-VA-tyel) - they say he is a good teacher. The same page gives В Канаде говорят по-французски (v ka-NA-dye ga-va-RYAT pa-fran-TSOOS-kee) - French is spoken in Canada - where the point is not hearsay but the generalising they, and the third plural therefore covers both somebody told me and people in general. Only context tells you which. Epistemic modality is the confidence scale, and the relevant reference defines it as a sub-type of linguistic modality that encompasses knowledge, belief, or credence in a proposition. It is realised grammatically, for example by modal verbs and moods, and non-grammatically, for example by adverbials such as perhaps and possibly. Russian uses both routes: наверное (na-VYER-na-ye, probably), может быть (MO-zhet byt, maybe), вероятно (vee-ra-YAT-na, in all likelihood), вряд ли (vryad lee, hardly, unlikely), едва ли (yed-VA lee, scarcely), маловероятно (MA-la-vee-ra-yat-na, unlikely). The German parallel in the same article shows how a language may mark hearsay with a modal verb: Er soll ein guter Schachspieler sein is glossed he is said to be a good chess player. Russian has no single verb doing that, so it uses говорят plus a что-clause or an adverbial, and learning which Russian frame corresponds to which degree of commitment is the practical skill. Two formal traps complete the picture. Должен means obligation, has to, while должно быть means deduction, it must be so - one letter of difference and a completely different modal meaning. And значит (ZNA-cheet, so, that means) introduces an inference the speaker has just drawn, which makes it a discourse marker of deduction rather than a word meaning means in the dictionary sense.
lessons.example: Read one short exchange and label every epistemic move. - Ты не знаешь, где Аня? - Кажется, она в библиотеке. Вчера она говорила, что будет готовиться к экзамену. - Неужели? Я думала, экзамен уже сдавали. - Возможно, я что-то путаю. Но, судя по расписанию на двери, экзамен в пятницу. - Значит, она готовится. - Вряд ли она уже закончила, если экзамен в пятницу. (ty nye ZNA-yesh, gdye A-nya? KA-zhet-sya, a-NA v beeb-lee-a-TYE-kye. fchee-RA a-NA ga-va-REE-la, shta BOO-det ga-TO-veet-sya k ek-za-MYE-noo. nee-oo-ZHE-lee? ya DOO-ma-la, ek-za-MYEN oo-ZHE sda-VA-lee. vaz-MOZH-na, ya SHTA-ta POO-ta-yoo. no, soo-DYA pa ras-pee-SA-nee-yoo na DVYE-ree, ek-za-MYEN v PYAT-nee-tsoo. ZNA-cheet, a-NA ga-TO-veet-sya. vryad lee a-NA oo-ZHE za-KON-chee-la, YE-slee ek-za-MYEN v PYAT-nee-tsoo.) Label the moves in order. Кажется is a low-commitment inference from indirect evidence - evidential, not certainty. Она говорила, что... is reported speech in the past with a future-in-the-past meaning, and it is hearsay with a named source, which makes it the strongest evidence in the exchange. Неужели is not an evidence claim at all but a marker of surprise that invites the other speaker to justify an assumption. Возможно softens the speaker's own reliability. Судя по расписанию is an inference from a document, which is inferential evidence of the cleanest kind. Значит presents a conclusion the speaker has just drawn from that evidence. Вряд ли introduces a negative likelihood judgement with a stated ground. Now convert the whole exchange to a written register and watch the hedges change shape: Вероятно, она находится в библиотеке. Согласно её словам, она готовится к экзамену, который, по данным расписания, состоится в пятницу. Маловероятно, что она уже завершила подготовку. (vee-ra-YAT-na, a-NA na-KHO-deet-sya v beeb-lee-a-TYE-kye. sag-LAS-na yeyo sla-VAM, a-NA ga-TO-veet-sya k ek-za-MYE-noo, ka-TO-ryy, pa DAN-nym ras-pee-SA-nee-ya, sa-sta-EET-sya v PYAT-nee-tsoo. MA-la-vee-ra-yat-na, shta a-NA oo-ZHE za-veer-SHEE-la pad-ga-TOF-koo.) The hedges have become fronted adverbials and prepositional phrases with deverbal nouns, and the personal source has become a formal attribution. Same content, higher register, and the confidence levels are still visible once you know where to look.
lessons.question: A Russian colleague writes Маловероятно, что она уже завершила подготовку. A learner translates it as: it is impossible that she has finished her preparation. What has gone wrong?
lessons.answer: Маловероятно is the lowest rung of the likelihood scale, not an impossibility; the translation overstates it. Unlikelihood leaves the possibility open, and the writer has chosen a hedge rather than a denial.
lessons.distractor: Nothing has gone wrong: мало- means little, so маловероятно means fully impossible, and the не- inside the clause restores the negation the learner thought was missing.
lessons.correction: Мало- in маловероятно means little, low - a low probability, not a zero. The scale runs from маловероятно through вряд ли and едва ли to может быть, вероятно and наверное, with должно быть at the confident-deduction end, and none of the lower steps asserts impossibility; for that Russian uses невозможно or не может быть. The second half of the distractor rests on a real misconception about negation: Russian marks negation on the clause or on the word, and its scope does not stack the way English not unlikely does, so завершила is simply the verb finished inside the что-clause and there is no second negation for it to interact with. If the writer had meant impossibility the frame and the confidence level of the sentence would both be much stronger than the ones on the page.

depth.definitions: Evidentiality: the marking of the nature of the evidence for a statement, whether direct (perceived by the speaker) or indirect (hearsay and inference). Quotative: a marker that information is reported from another speaker, for example говорят. Inferential: a marker that the speaker has deduced the statement from evidence, for example судя по and по-видимому. Epistemic modality: the sub-type of modality that concerns knowledge, belief or credence in a proposition, that is, a confidence scale. Mirative: a marker of surprise at information that is new to the speaker, for example оказывается and неужели. Discourse marker: a small word that organises the relation between parts of a text; значит introduces a conclusion just drawn. Deverbal noun: used here for the written-register hedges such as вероятность and данные. Prerequisite: reported speech from lesson 76, the hedging adverbials наверное, кажется, может быть and пожалуй from lesson 77, and the third-plural passive from lesson 83.
depth.mechanism: This material matters because evidentiality and epistemic modality are independent axes, and Russian encodes them with different words, so a reader must track both at once. Source of knowledge answers who told you; degree of confidence answers how much will you bet. The four useful combinations are a named source plus high confidence (Она говорила, что...), an unnamed source plus moderate confidence (Говорят, что...), direct evidence plus an inference (Судя по расписанию...), and no evidence plus low confidence (Может быть, я ошибаюсь). Getting these right is what lets you disagree with a text appropriately: you cannot refute a hearsay report as if it were the writer's own claim, and you must not read a hedge as a commitment. Mechanically Russian performs all of this lexically rather than morphologically, with two consequences. First, position matters: sentence-initial adverbials such as вероятно and по-видимому scope over the whole following clause, whereas the same word inside the clause may scope only over a phrase. Second, the written register prefers prepositional phrases built on deverbal nouns (по данным, согласно отчёту) where the spoken register prefers verbs (говорят, пишут). The limits are real. Russian has no evidential inflection, so the same sentence can be honestly reported as hearsay by one speaker and asserted by another, and only context disambiguates. And a reader should not treat a hedge in Russian academic prose as proof of weak commitment, because hedging there is also a politeness convention rather than a probability statement.
depth.secondExample: Take one fact and move it down the confidence scale, noticing that each step also changes the evidence claimed. The fact is that the factory is closing. Говорят, завод закрывают. (ga-va-RYAT, za-VOT zak-ry-VA-yut.) - unnamed hearsay in the third plural. По-видимому, завод закрывают. (pa-VEE-dee-ma-moo, za-VOT zak-ry-VA-yut.) - an inference from what the speaker can see or hear, with no named source. Судя по объявлениям, завод закрывают. (soo-DYA pa ab-yav-LYE-nee-yam, za-VOT zak-ry-VA-yut.) - inference from a named kind of evidence. Оказывается, завод закрывают. (a-KA-zy-va-yet-sya, za-VOT zak-ry-VA-yut.) - news to the speaker, marked as newly learned. Должно быть, завод закрывают. (dolzh-NO byt, za-VOT zak-ry-VA-yut.) - a confident deduction from indirect evidence. Вряд ли завод закрывают. (vryad lee za-VOT zak-ry-VA-yut.) - a judgement against the proposition. Finally the committed assertion with no hedge at all: Завод закрывают. Notice that the tense and aspect of the core clause never change; all the work is done by the frame. That is why epistemic Russian can be learned as a set of fixed openers plus a normal clause, and why the same opener will appear in dozens of otherwise unrelated sentences.
depth.mistake: The most damaging error is to confuse obligation with deduction. Должен in Он должен прийти means he has to come; должно быть in Он, должно быть, пришёл means he must have come. A learner who reads the deduction as an obligation will systematically misinterpret written reports, where должно было and должно быть carry the writer's inference and say nothing about anyone's duty. The diagnostic is the form: должен, должна and должны agree with a subject and mean obligation, while должно быть is invariable and means deduction. The second error is to translate говорят as a specific third party. Cornell glosses it as it is said, one says, they say, and the sentence has no subject, so reading in a named group is an addition rather than a translation. The third error is to flatten the whole scale into maybe. Может быть, вероятно, по-видимому, должно быть and вряд ли mark genuinely different levels, and a reader who reduces them to one hedge loses the writer's information about how much is actually known.
depth.application: Task: you have four pieces of information about a delayed train - a platform announcement, a fellow passenger's guess, a message from a friend, and your own reading of the timetable board. Write one Russian sentence for each that marks the evidence type and the confidence correctly, using a different frame each time, then gloss each sentence in English. Model response: (1) Объявление сообщает, что поезд задерживается на двадцать минут. (2) По-видимому, поезд задерживается. (3) Мне написали, что поезд задерживается. (4) Судя по табло, поезд задерживается на двадцать минут. Glosses: (1) the announcement reports a twenty-minute delay - named source, high confidence; (2) apparently the train is delayed - inference, moderate confidence; (3) I was written to that the train is delayed - hearsay through a named channel; (4) judging by the board, the train is twenty minutes late - direct evidence, high confidence. Self-review rubric: (1) does each sentence use a different evidential frame? (2) is the confidence level of each gloss carried by the frame rather than by your own knowledge of the facts? (3) have you avoided должен where you meant должно быть? Three yes answers passes; then repeat the task using only hearsay frames and note how repetitive the register becomes.
depth.summary: Russian marks two independent things: where information came from (evidentiality, through говорят, судя по, оказывается and по-видимому) and how much the speaker will commit to it (epistemic modality, through может быть, вероятно, наверное, должно быть and вряд ли). Because the frames are lexical, they sit outside the core clause and leave its tense and aspect untouched, which is what makes them learnable as a set. The two formal traps to keep in view are должен against должно быть, and говорят against a named source. One limitation to respect is that hedges can be politeness conventions as much as probability statements, so they should not be over-read as weakness of commitment in academic prose. The next lesson turns to the other half of spoken interaction, expressing and defending an opinion without damaging the person you are talking to.

visual.title: Two-axis grid for placing a hedged Russian sentence: evidence source against confidence
visual.description: A labelled grid rendered as steps. One axis is how you know (direct, inference, hearsay, nothing) and the other is how strongly the speaker commits (low, moderate, confident deduction, assertion), with the Russian frame that occupies each cell.
steps: Axis check - Ask two questions of the sentence before translating: where did this information come from, and how much is the speaker betting on it? Answer both first.
Cell 1 - Direct evidence plus high commitment: no hedge, plus a verb of perception. Example: Я вижу, что поезд стоит на втором пути - I can see the train is standing on platform two.
Cell 2 - Inference plus moderate commitment: по-видимому, похоже, судя по plus a noun. Example: Судя по табло, поезд задерживается - judging by the board, the train is delayed.

Cell 3 - Unnamed hearsay plus moderate commitment: говорят, пишут, сообщается. Example: Говорят, завод закрывают - they say the factory is closing. The third plural implies human sources and names none.

Cell 4 - Confident deduction from indirect evidence: должно быть, очевидно, значит, получается. Example: Должно быть, она уже дома - she must be home by now. Check that it is not должен plus an infinitive, which would be obligation.

Cell 5 - Low or negative commitment: может быть, возможно, вряд ли, едва ли, маловероятно. Example: Вряд ли она уже закончила - she is unlikely to have finished already. These are judgements, not denials.

russianItems.meaning: apparently, evidently (an inference with no named source)
judging by (takes the dative; inference from named evidence)
it must be, presumably (a confident deduction, not an obligation)
it turns out, it appears (marks news newly learned by the speaker)
it follows, it comes out that (an inference just drawn)
hardly, unlikely (a negative judgement, not a denial)
scarcely, hardly (a slightly more bookish twin of вряд ли)
it is unlikely, improbable (low probability, not impossibility)
really? (marks surprise and invites the other speaker to justify an assumption)
it seems, it looks as if
so, that means (introduces a conclusion just drawn)
according to the data of (a written-register attribution)

lessons.title: Opinions, agreement and disagreement: saying no without doing damage
lessons.explanation: Russian has a rich and slightly formal apparatus for disagreeing, and the reason is not mere politeness for its own sake; it is that disagreement is a social act with costs that speakers manage deliberately. Politeness theory gives you the framework: it centres on the notion of politeness construed as efforts to redress the affronts to a person's public self-image or face, it distinguishes positive face (the want to be approved of) from negative face (the want to be unimpeded), and it names the face-threatening act as the unit to be managed. The same source notes that the model has been challenged, including on cross-cultural applicability, so treat it as a useful map rather than a law of nature. Speech-act theory supplies the other half: an utterance does not merely describe, it performs - Austin's performatives and the categories of apologising, promising, ordering, requesting, refusing and complaining - so a disagreement in Russian is a refusal-type act, and its wording is part of the act itself. From Cornell comes the single most practical Russian device. The negative particle не is commonly used to make a question less abrupt or to turn it into a polite request, as in Ты не знаешь, где живёт Аня? (ty nye ZNA-yesh, gdye zhee-VYOT A-nya) - do you happen to know where Anya lives? - and Извините, вы мне не поможете? (eez-vee-NEE-tye, vy mnye nye pa-MO-zhe-tye) - excuse me, could you help me? The mechanism is that adding не to a request presents it as an inquiry rather than a demand, which reduces the pressure on the listener's freedom of action. Russian uses the same logic in disagreement. The polite-imperative material shows the second device: the imperfective imperative is used because you are merely telling the person to start doing something rather than to get it done, which is why a host says Садитесь rather than Сядьте. In an argument, the parallel move is to attack the proposition rather than to instruct the person: это спорный вопрос (EH-ta SPOR-nyy vap-ROS, that is a debatable question) rather than вы ошибаетесь (vy a-shee-BA-ye-tyes, you are mistaken). The working set of frames is small and worth learning as chunks. To state an opinion: по-моему (pa-MO-ye-moo, in my opinion), на мой взгляд (na moy vzglyad, in my view), мне кажется (mnye KA-zhet-sya, it seems to me), я считаю (ya shchee-TA-yoo, I consider), с моей точки зрения (s ma-YEY TOCH-kee ZRYE-nee-ya, from my point of view). To agree: я согласен or я согласна (ya sag-LA-syen, ya sag-LAS-na, I agree - masculine and feminine forms), вы правы (vy PRA-vy, you are right), совершенно верно (sa-veer-SHEN-na VYER-na, quite right), не могу не согласиться (nye ma-GOO nye sag-la-SEET-sya, I cannot but agree). To disagree without damage: это спорный вопрос, я не совсем согласен (ya nye saf-SYEM sag-LA-syen, I do not entirely agree), мне трудно согласиться (mnye TROOD-na sag-la-SEET-sya, I find it hard to agree), разрешите не согласиться (raz-ree-SHEE-tye nye sag-la-SEET-sya, allow me to disagree), and the two-part construction с одной стороны ... с другой стороны. The single most effective Russian disagreement pattern is concession first: Я понимаю вашу точку зрения, но... (ya pa-nee-MA-yoo VA-shoo TOCH-koo ZRYE-nee-ya, no...) - I understand your point of view, but... This grants the interlocutor's positive face before the objection is delivered, and it is the pattern you should default to in any disagreement with a colleague or a stranger.
lessons.example: Read a disagreement conducted badly and then well. Bad version: - Я думаю, что работать дома лучше. - Нет, вы не правы. Дома работать нельзя. (- ya DOO-ma-yoo, shto ra-BO-tat DO-ma LOOT-she. - NYET, vy nye PRA-vy. DO-ma ra-BO-tat NYEL-zya.) - I think working at home is better. - No, you are wrong. You cannot work at home. Good version: - Я думаю, что работать дома лучше. - По-моему, это спорный вопрос. С одной стороны, дома никто не мешает, а с другой стороны, не всякую работу можно делать дома. Я не совсем согласен, что дома всегда лучше. - На мой взгляд, вы правы насчёт не всякой работы. Но мне кажется, что для моей работы это идеальный вариант. (pa-MO-ye-moo, EH-ta SPOR-nyy vap-ROS. s ad-NOY sta-ra-NY, DO-ma neek-TO nye mye-SHA-yet, a z droo-GOY sta-ra-NY, nye FSYA-koo-yoo ra-BO-too MOZH-na DYE-lat DO-ma. ya nye saf-SYEM sag-LA-syen, shta DO-ma vsyeg-DA LOOT-she. na moy vzglyad, vy PRA-vy na-SHCHOT nye FSYA-kay ra-BO-ty. no mnye KA-zhet-sya, shta dlya ma-YEY ra-BO-ty EH-ta ee-dee-AL-nyy va-ree-ANT.) - In my opinion that is a debatable question. On the one hand, at home nobody disturbs you, and on the other hand not every kind of work can be done at home. I do not entirely agree that home is always better. - In my view you are right about not every kind of work. But it seems to me that for my work it is the ideal option. Compare the two exchanges closely. In the bad version, the second speaker produces two face-threatening moves in a row: a flat нет and an accusation of error (вы не правы), followed by an impersonal prohibition that ends the discussion. In the good version, the second speaker does five things: she frames her own contribution as an opinion rather than a correction (по-моему), she converts the whole question into a debatable one (спорный вопрос), she gives both sides explicitly (с одной стороны ... с другой стороны), she disagrees with a hedge rather than a verdict (я не совсем согласен), and she agrees with the part of the first speaker's claim that she can accept. The first speaker then reciprocates with на мой взгляд and вы правы насчёт..., which concedes a point before defending her position. Note what has not changed: nobody's factual claim has been abandoned, and the second speaker still holds that not every job can be done at home. Politeness here is not the abandonment of content; it is the packaging of content so that the other person can keep arguing. Note also that the good version is longer - roughly twice as long - and that this length is the cost of the repair. A learner who wants to be both polite and brief in Russian has to accept that brevity in disagreement sounds like a verdict.
lessons.question: You must tell a colleague in a meeting that you do not accept his proposal, and you want to keep the working relationship intact. Which Russian move best matches the politeness logic described in this lesson?
lessons.answer: Concede the part you accept and then hedge the objection: Я понимаю вашу точку зрения, но я не совсем согласен с этим предложением - I understand your point of view, but I do not entirely agree with this proposal.
lessons.distractor: State the objection impersonally so that no person is addressed: Это предложение нельзя принять, потому что оно не работает - this proposal cannot be accepted because it does not work.
lessons.correction: The impersonal form looks neutral, but it is not polite in the relevant sense. A face-threatening act is a threat to the person you are addressing, and an impersonal verdict removes the interlocutor's room to respond while still coming from you; Russian speakers read нельзя принять as a closed decision, not as an opinion offered for discussion. The hedge я не совсем согласен does the opposite: it presents a position as the speaker's own view, which invites a reply, and the concessive opener Я понимаю вашу точку зрения acknowledges the colleague's standing before the objection lands. Impersonal constructions themselves are not rude - lesson 83 showed how useful they are in reports - but they are the wrong tool for a disagreement between two people who have to keep working together.

depth.definitions: Face: a person's public self-image. Positive face: the want that one's wants be approved of. Negative face: the want that one's actions be unimpeded. Face-threatening act (FTA): an act such as a request, a criticism or a refusal that damages face. Redress: the linguistic work done to soften an FTA. Speech act: an utterance that performs an action rather than merely describing one; refusing and disagreeing are speech acts. Hedge: a modifier that lowers commitment or force, for example не совсем and мне кажется. Concessive opener: a clause that grants something before an objection, for example Я понимаю вашу точку зрения, но... Prerequisite: opinion frames and reported speech from lessons 76 and 77, the particle не in polite requests from lesson 77, and the aspect choice in polite imperatives from lesson 85.
depth.mechanism: Russian politeness in disagreement operates by redistributing two things: who owns the claim, and who has the right to close the topic. Ownership is moved by opinion frames. Я думаю, что... presents a claim as the speaker's belief, and this is important grammatically, because a что-clause after a verb of thinking keeps the assertion inside the speaker's scope rather than in the world. Russian does not shift tenses in that clause the way English does, so the frame is doing more work than an English equivalent would. Closing rights are moved by hedges and by the two-sided construction. С одной стороны ... с другой стороны presents the question as having two admissible answers, which denies nobody the right to reply; я не совсем согласен leaves the door open by degree rather than by verdict. The negative particle supplies a third mechanism specific to Russian: putting не in a question or request converts a demand into an inquiry, which is a negative-face repair, and it is so productive that it appears in service encounters, requests for directions and offers, as in Не желаете ли печенья? The limits are worth stating plainly. Politeness theory has been criticised for assuming that its strategies are universal, and Russian conventions differ from English ones in specific ways: directness between friends is warmer than hedging, and a close friend may find я не совсем согласен cold rather than courteous. There is also a gender dimension in the agreement forms themselves, since согласен and согласна, уверен and уверена, must match the speaker. And over-hedging has its own cost: a speaker who prefaces every contribution with мне кажется and по-моему in a context that expects a position will seem evasive, and in Russian work settings directness on the substance is usually welcome once the frame has been softened once.
depth.secondExample: Run the same apparatus on a refusal rather than a disagreement, which is where Russian politeness conventions are most visible. Blunt refusal: Нет, я не могу. I cannot. Once-hedged refusal: К сожалению, я не смогу. (k sa-zha-LYE-nee-yoo, ya nye sma-GOO.) Unfortunately I will not be able to manage it. Fully redressed refusal: К сожалению, я не смогу прийти в субботу. Может быть, в воскресенье? Или давайте перенесём на следующую неделю. (k sa-zha-LYE-nee-yoo, ya nye sma-GOO pree-TEE f soo-BO-too. MO-zhet byt, v vas-kree-SYE-nee-ye? EE-lee dav-VAY-tye pee-ree-nye-SYOM na SLYE-doo-yoo-shchoo-yoo nee-DYE-lyoo.) Unfortunately I will not be able to come on Saturday. Maybe Sunday? Or let us move it to next week. The repair here has three parts: an apology token (к сожалению), a refusal that does not deny the relationship, and an alternative. The alternative is the crucial move, because it converts a refusal into a counter-proposal and preserves the interlocutor's positive face. Notice that давайте plus a perfective non-past (перенесём) is the standard way to propose joint action, and that the offer of two options rather than one leaves the other speaker with a real choice. Compare with the English habit of adding an apology several times; Russian usually marks the regret once, with к сожалению or боюсь, что... and then spends its effort on the alternative.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to translate English directness word for word. Нет, вы не правы and Это неправильно are grammatical Russian and they do mean what they say, but delivered to a colleague or a stranger they read as a verdict and can close a discussion; a learner who wonders why a Russian counterpart has gone quiet has often simply issued a verdict where an opinion frame was expected. The diagnostic is to ask which of the two the sentence is: a statement about the world, or a statement about your view. Verbs of thinking and opinion frames convert the first into the second. The second error is the opposite and more insidious for a learner: hedging so much that no position is stated. Мне кажется, что, возможно, это иногда не совсем... is not polite Russian, it is an unfinished sentence, and Russian interlocutors will press for a position rather than reward the hedging. The third error is register and address. Disagreeing with an unfamiliar adult using ты forms, or with the blunt imperative Ты не прав, combines the wrong pronoun with the wrong speech act; use the вы forms until the relationship justifies the shift, and remember that the negative-particle request (Вы не скажете...?) is a politeness device you can reuse in almost any service situation.
depth.application: Task: write a four-turn Russian exchange in which you state an opinion about whether students should take a gap year, your partner disagrees, you defend your position while conceding one point, and your partner accepts part of your argument. Then mark every politeness device you used and label it positive-face, negative-face or opinion-framing. Model response, opening turn: На мой взгляд, год перерыва после школы полезен, потому что человек успевает понять, чего он хочет. Partner: По-моему, это спорный вопрос. С одной стороны, опыт полезен, но, с другой стороны, многие теряют привычку учиться. Я не совсем с вами согласен. You: Понимаю вашу точку зрения, и насчёт привычки вы правы. Но мне кажется, что мотивация важнее. Labelled devices: на мой взгляд and по-моему (opinion framing), спорный вопрос (negative-face repair, keeps the topic open), с одной стороны ... с другой стороны (two-sided construction), я не совсем с вами согласен (hedged disagreement), Понимаю вашу точку зрения and вы правы насчёт... (positive-face concession), но мне кажется (opinion framing again). Self-review rubric: (1) does every disagreement contain at least one opinion frame or hedge? (2) is there at least one explicit concession before an objection? (3) are the address forms consistent (вы throughout, or ты throughout, with a reason)? Three yes answers passes; if any answer is no, revise the framework rather than the vocabulary.
depth.summary: Politeness in Russian disagreement is a system, not a set of nice phrases. Framing devices move a claim from the world into the speaker's view, hedges keep the topic open, the two-sided construction denies nobody the right to reply, and a concessive opener protects the other person before the objection arrives. Cornell's negative particle supplies the Russian-specific repair for requests, and the imperfective polite imperative supplies the same logic for instructions. Keep three limits in view: politeness conventions vary across cultures and within Russian by relationship, the agreement adjectives must match the speaker's gender, and over-hedging costs you your position. The next lesson turns the same imperative apparatus in the other direction, from managing a person to describing a process step by step out loud.

visual.title: Four-move repair sequence for a disagreement, with the Russian frame for each move
visual.description: A labelled sequence that takes one disagreement from its blunt form to its fully redressed form in four ordered moves, naming the frame used and the face concern it addresses.
steps: Move 0 - The blunt version, for contrast. Нет, вы не правы. This is grammatical, means exactly what it says, and ends the exchange. Keep it as a baseline so you can see what the later moves are buying.
Move 1 - Frame the claim as yours, not as a fact. Add по-моему, на мой взгляд or мне кажется. Effect: the statement becomes an opinion, which is a claim you can revise without losing face.

Move 2 - Open the topic instead of closing it. Add это спорный вопрос or the pair с одной стороны ... с другой стороны. Effect: the interlocutor keeps the right to answer, which is the negative-face repair.

Move 3 - Concede before objecting. Я понимаю вашу точку зрения, но... or вы правы насчёт..., но... Effect: the other person's standing is acknowledged before the objection arrives, which is the positive-face repair.

Move 4 - Hedge the objection rather than issuing a verdict. я не совсем согласен, мне трудно согласиться, разрешите не согласиться. Effect: the disagreement is stated as a degree rather than as a judgement on the person.

Verification - Count your moves. If a disagreement contains none of moves 1 to 4, it is a verdict. If it contains three or four in a row before any content, you have over-hedged and the position has disappeared.

lessons.title: Describing a process out loud: building a spoken procedure step by step
lessons.explanation: You can already read a procedure; this lesson teaches you to produce one aloud, which is a different skill because speech must be ordered in real time and cannot be re-read. The grammatical core is the imperative, and its formation is rule-governed rather than arbitrary. Cornell states the working rule as follows: add -и (stressed) to the non-past stem if its stress pattern is E or M, and add -й to vowel-final stems and -ь to consonant-final stems if the stress pattern is S, then add -те for the вы form. The page's own table shows позвонить giving позвони, спросить giving спроси, открыть giving открой and поставить giving поставь, with the вы forms позвоните, спросите, откройте, поставьте. Cornell also gives the fuller set of conditions and, importantly, a list of common irregulars: ехать gives поезжай, дать gives дай, есть gives ешь, давать gives давай, пить gives пей and стоять gives стой. Learn the six irregulars as chunks, because they are among the most frequent verbs in instructions and they are the ones you cannot derive. General linguistics frames what you are doing: the imperative mood is a grammatical mood that forms a command or request, it is typically found only in the present tense and second person, and it is one of the irrealis moods, that is, a mood of unrealised interpretation. The comparison worth holding in mind is that some other languages have first- and third-person imperatives with the meanings let us do something and let them do something - Russian has a partial equivalent in давайте plus a verb, which you will use in lesson 90 - but the working second-person imperative is what carries almost all procedural speech. Sequencing is the second half of the skill, and it is done by adverbs rather than by grammar: сначала (sna-CHA-la, at first), затем (za-TYEM, then, next), далее (DA-lye, further, next), после этого (POS-lye EH-ta-va, after that), в конце (v kan-TSYE, at the end), шаг за шагом (shag za SHA-gam, step by step), plus numbering by во-первых and во-вторых when the steps are parallel rather than sequential. You also need a neutral alternative to the imperative, because instructions addressed to nobody in particular are commoner in Russian technical writing than in English. Two impersonal frames do that work: нужно or следует or необходимо plus the infinitive, as in Затем нужно добавить воду (za-TYEM NOOZH-na da-BAV-eet va-DOO, then one must add water), and the -ся middle, as in Вода добавляется после кипения (va-DA da-bav-LYA-yet-sya POS-lye kee-PYE-nee-ya, the water is added after boiling). Both remove the second person entirely, which is exactly what a manual or a lab protocol wants. Finally, register control. The -те form is the default for any audience that is not a close friend, including one stranger and any group; Cornell notes that for an even stronger command an infinitive may be used, which is why signs and trainers say Сидеть! rather than the imperative. Use the infinitive deliberately as a signal of institutional authority, not accidentally. Aspect in procedure is covered in lesson 85, and the two lessons must be used together: the form tells you how to build the imperative, and the aspect tells you whether each step means do it once, keep doing it, or never do it. Two terms frame everything that follows: повелительное наклонение (pa-vee-LEE-tyel-na-ye nak-la-NYE-nee-ye) is the imperative mood, and поезжайте (pa-yez-ZHAY-tye) is the irregular imperative of ехать, the form you use whenever you tell somebody to travel by vehicle.
lessons.example: Here is a spoken procedure written the way a competent speaker would actually deliver it, with the sequencing and the form choices marked. Сначала включите питание и подождите две минуты. Затем проверьте, горит ли зелёная лампочка. Если она не горит, нажмите кнопку ещё раз. Далее откройте крышку и поставьте деталь на место. После этого закройте крышку и поверните ключ на четверть оборота. В конце убедитесь, что лампочка горит. (sna-CHA-la vlyoo-CHEE-tye pee-TA-nee-ye ee pa-dazh-DEE-tye dva mee-NOO-ty. za-TYEM pra-VYER-tye, ga-REET lee zye-LYO-na-ya LAM-pach-ka. YE-slee a-NA nye ga-REET, nazh-MEE-tye KNOP-koo yash-SHCHO raz. DA-lye at-KROY-tye KRYSH-koo ee pa-STAV-tye dye-TAL na MYE-sta. POS-lye EH-ta-va zak-ROY-tye KRYSH-koo ee pa-veer-NEE-tye klyooch na CHYET-veert a-ba-RO-ta. v kan-TSYE oo-bee-DEE-tyes, shta LAM-pach-ka ga-REET.) First switch on the power and wait two minutes. Then check whether the green lamp is on. If it is not on, press the button once more. Next open the cover and put the part in place. After that close the cover and turn the key a quarter turn. At the end make sure that the lamp is on. Now examine the choices. Eight imperatives, all in the -те form and all perfective, because every step is a bounded action to be completed once: включите, подождите, проверьте, нажмите, откройте, поставьте, закройте, поверните. Two of these reward attention: поставьте is built from the поставить stem with -ь plus -те and is the commonest instruction verb in Russian workshops, and подождите comes from the irregular family you memorised rather than from the general rule. Note the indirect question горит ли, which uses the ли particle you met in lesson 76 rather than a that-clause, because the operator is asked to determine a yes-no state rather than to receive a statement. Note also that the ordering is carried entirely by four adverbs and one conditional clause, with no tense anywhere in the imperatives. Now do the same thing in the neutral impersonal register, as a manual would print it: Сначала включается питание и нужно подождать две минуты. Затем проверяется, горит ли зелёная лампочка. Далее крышка открывается и деталь ставится на место. В конце нужно убедиться, что лампочка горит. (sna-CHA-la fklyoo-CHA-yet-sya pee-TA-nee-ye ee NOOZH-na pa-dazh-DAT dva mee-NOO-ty. za-TYEM pra-vye-RYA-yet-sya, ga-REET lee zye-LYO-na-ya LAM-pach-ka. DA-lye KRYSH-ka at-kry-VA-yet-sya ee dye-TAL STAV-eet-sya na MYE-sta. v kan-TSYE NOOZH-na oo-bee-DEET-sya, shta LAM-pach-ka ga-REET.) The steps are identical, the aspect is preserved, the second person has disappeared, and the text has become printable. Choosing between the two registers is a decision about who is responsible for the performance, not about politeness.
lessons.question: You are explaining a four-step process to a group of visitors you have just met. Which instruction is the best choice for the first step, and why?
lessons.answer: Возьмите карту и посмотрите на схему - take the map and look at the diagram - because both verbs are in the вы form with -те, which is the default for any audience that is not a close friend.
lessons.distractor: Возьми карту и посмотри на схему - because the singular imperative is shorter and therefore easier to follow in speech.
lessons.correction: The form without -те addresses one person informally, so with a group of visitors it is both the wrong number and the wrong register; Russian listeners notice the missing -те immediately and read it as either an error or an unintended claim of familiarity. Length is not the criterion: comprehensibility in speech comes from clear sequencing and one instruction per sentence, not from shortening the verb. Note also that возьмите is one of the forms you must memorise, since брать gives возьми rather than a form derivable from the non-past stem alone, and its perfective partner взять supplies возьмите for a single completed act.

depth.definitions: Imperative mood: the mood that forms a command or request; typically present tense and second person, and one of the irrealis moods. Non-past stem: the stem used for present and future forms, from which the imperative is built. Вы form: the imperative with -те added, used for one person politely and for any group. Irregular imperative: a form not derivable from the general rules, for example поезжай, дай, ешь, давай, пей, стой. Sequencing adverb: a word that orders steps, for example сначала, затем, далее, после этого, в конце. Impersonal frame: нужно, следует or необходимо plus an infinitive, or a -ся form, which removes the second person. Register: here the choice between addressing the performer and describing the operation. Prerequisite: imperative forms and aspect in commands from lessons 69 and 85, the ли particle from lesson 76, and the verbal-noun and passive material from lessons 83 and 84 for the impersonal version.
depth.mechanism: A spoken procedure is a genre with its own constraints, and the constraints explain the grammar. First, speech is linear and unrepeatable, so each step must be short and self-contained; a Russian speaker consequently uses one imperative per sentence and puts the sequencer first. Second, the listener's memory is the bottleneck, so the number of steps in flight must stay small, which is why далее and после этого are so frequent and why parallel steps are kept aspectually parallel. Third, responsibility must be assigned, and this is where the register decision lives: an imperative with -те assigns the performance to the listener, while нужно plus the infinitive or a -ся form attributes it to nobody and describes the operation itself. Russian manuals prefer the second, spoken demonstrations prefer the first. Cornell's formation material is reliable but incomplete on its own, which is why it appears twice, once as a rule of thumb keyed to stress patterns E, M and S and once as the fuller condition set involving vowel-final stems, end stress, consonant clusters and щ. The practical consequence is that you should learn the rule, memorise the six irregulars as vocabulary, and still expect a small residue of verbs to surprise you. Two further limits matter. The imperative has no tense, so a procedure cannot by itself locate its steps in time; that comes from the sequencers and the context, and a procedure delivered in the past tense stops being a procedure and becomes a report. And the infinitive command, which Cornell notes is stronger than any imperative, is institutionally marked: it belongs on signs and in trainers' mouths, and a colleague who uses it with you is being deliberately curt.
depth.secondExample: Take the same process and deliver it to a single close friend, then to a written manual, and watch three separate changes rather than one. To a friend: Слушай, сначала включи питание и подожди две минуты. Потом проверь, горит ли лампочка. Если не горит, нажми кнопку ещё раз. Открой крышку, поставь деталь, закрой и поверни ключ. В конце убедись, что лампочка горит. (SHLOO-shay, sna-CHA-la fklyoo-CHEE pee-TA-nee-ye ee pa-dazh-DEE dva mee-NOO-ty. pa-TOM pra-VYER, ga-REET lee LAM-pach-ka. YE-slee nye ga-REET, nazh-MEE KNOP-koo yash-SHCHO raz. at-KROY KRYSH-koo, pa-STAV dye-TAL, zak-ROY ee pa-veer-NEE klyooch. v kan-TSYE oo-bee-DEES, shta LAM-pach-ka ga-REET.) Change one: the -те is gone, and with it the social distance. Change two: the sequencers become colloquial (потом rather than затем and далее), and the opening particle слушай marks a conversational frame that a printed manual can never use. Change three: the sentences get shorter and some connectives disappear, because in speech the delivery itself carries the ordering. The content is identical in all three versions - friend, visitors, manual - and the grammar has moved from informal second person singular, through polite second person plural, to a subjectless impersonal. That three-way movement is the core production skill of this lesson, and it is the reverse of the reading work in lesson 82, where the same movement ran from written to spoken.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to produce a procedure in the past tense. A learner who says Сначала я включил питание, потом я проверил лампочку has told a story about themselves, not given instructions, and a Russian listener will wait for the instruction that never arrives. The diagnostic is simple: a procedure contains no first-person subject and no past tense unless it is quoting a condition. The second error is forgetting -те in front of a group or a stranger, which is read as either a mistake or unintended familiarity. The third is form-level and very common in live speech: building the imperative from the wrong stem, most often from the infinitive or the first person singular. Remember that Cornell's rule keys off the non-past stem with its stress pattern, so открою gives открой and поставлю gives поставь, not открыть and поставить. The fourth error is aspect drift inside a procedure: mixing варите and сварите across parallel steps produces a text in which some steps are bounded and others are not, which is exactly the information the listener needs and the speaker has thrown away. Keep parallel steps parallel unless the step is deliberately iterative, as in помешивайте.
depth.application: Task: choose a process you can perform but cannot easily read back from notes - making a particular dish, changing a printer cartridge, or setting up a piece of equipment. Record yourself delivering it twice: once to a group using -те imperatives, and once in the impersonal register with нужно and -ся forms. Then listen and score yourself against three criteria. Model response, first two steps of the group version: Сначала снимите крышку и выньте старый картридж. Затем возьмите новый картридж и снимите защитную ленту. (sna-CHA-la snee-MEE-tye KRYSH-koo ee VYN-tye STA-ryy kar-TREEDJ. za-TYEM vaz-MEE-tye NO-vyy kar-TREEDJ ee snee-MEE-tye za-SHCHEET-noo-yoo LYEON-too.) Self-review rubric: (1) is every instruction in a consistent address form, with -те throughout for the group? (2) does every step begin with a sequencer, and is each step a single bounded action rather than two? (3) did you avoid the past tense and any first-person subject? Three yes answers passes. Then re-record only the steps you failed, because the failure will usually be a lapse of address form under the pressure of live delivery rather than a gap in knowledge.
depth.summary: Producing a spoken procedure requires three decisions made repeatedly and quickly: the imperative form, the aspect of each step, and the register that assigns responsibility. Cornell's formation rules plus the six irregulars cover the forms; lesson 85's aspect test covers the steps; and the choice between -те imperatives and impersonal нужно or -ся frames covers the register. Sequencing is lexical and therefore learnable as a list, and the gerund and verbal-noun material from lessons 72 and 84 lets you compress steps when a procedure must be written rather than spoken. The limits to carry forward are that the imperative carries no tense, that the infinitive command is institutionally marked rather than neutral, and that the polite-imperative pattern is idiomatic rather than freely productive in technical registers. The next lesson moves from producing a procedure to producing a summary, which needs the same control plus the discipline of retelling in your own words.

visual.title: Procedure-production pipeline: five decisions from process to spoken steps
visual.description: A labelled sequence of five decisions applied to one process, each naming the choice to make and the Russian form it produces. Text steps, not video.
steps: Decision 1 - Set the register. Who performs the steps: a named listener (use -те imperatives), a general reader (use нужно plus infinitive or -ся forms), or an institution speaking (infinitive commands such as Сидеть!). Everything else follows from this.

Decision 2 - Choose the form. Build each imperative from the non-past stem with Cornell's stress-pattern rule, then add -те if a listener is addressed. Check the six irregulars (поезжай, дай, ешь, давай, пей, стой) before trusting any derived form.

Decision 3 - Choose the aspect. Ask whether the step is completed once (perfective), kept going (iterative imperfective) or prohibited (imperfective under negation). Keep parallel steps aspectually parallel.
Decision 4 - Order the steps. Prefix each with a sequencer: сначала, затем, далее, после этого, в конце. Use во-первых and во-вторых only for parallel items rather than sequential steps.

Decision 5 - Set conditions and checks. Use если plus a finite verb for a condition, and an indirect question with ли for a state to be verified (проверьте, горит ли лампочка). Then stop: more than five or six steps in one breath needs splitting.

lessons.title: Summarising aloud in your own words: paraphrase, attribution and compression
lessons.explanation: A summary is a specific product with a specific name in linguistics, and knowing what it is makes it easier to do. A paraphrase or rephrase is a rewording of a text that retains the original meaning, and the same reference gives the everyday version: when someone tells a story they have heard, they paraphrase it in their own words while preserving the meaning. An abstract, the written cousin of the spoken summary, is a brief summary of a research article or other long text, often used to help the reader quickly ascertain the paper's purpose, and it may act as a stand-alone entity rather than a pointer into the full text. Two consequences follow for the oral task. First, your own words are part of the definition, not a stylistic preference: a summary that reuses the source's phrasing is a chain of quotations with the connective tissue removed. Second, a summary must be able to stand alone, which means it needs its own internal cohesion rather than the source's. That is where the linguistics of cohesion becomes practical advice. Cohesion is the grammatical and lexical linking within a text that holds it together, and Halliday and Hasan identify five categories of cohesive device: reference, ellipsis, substitution, lexical cohesion and conjunction. When you summarise, you deliberately break the source's chains and rebuild them: a pronoun chain that pointed back through five sentences becomes a named noun in your version, and an elliptical sentence becomes a full one. The device that matters most for spoken Russian is the correlative construction with то, что, which Cornell treats as obligatory with certain verbs and predicative expressions. It is what lets you summary-type a fact rather than a clause: Он говорил о том, что ремонт начнётся в мае (on ga-va-REEL a TOM, shta ree-MONT nach-NYOT-sya v MA-ye) - he spoke about the fact that the repair would begin in May - and Она довольна тем, что я хорошо работаю (a-NA da-VOL-na tyem, shta ya ha-ra-SHO ra-BO-ta-yoo) - she is pleased that I work well. Without the то, the sentence refuses to form with these verbs. For spoken delivery you need a small set of framing formulas, and they are worth learning as whole chunks. To open: В тексте говорится о том, что... (v TYEK-stye ga-va-REET-sya a TOM, shta) - the text says that...; Автор утверждает, что... (A-f tar oot-veerzh-DA-yet, shta) - the author asserts that...; Речь идёт о том, что... (ryech ee-DYOT a TOM, shta) - what is at issue is that... To compress: Главная мысль в том, что... (GLAV-na-ya mysl v tom, shta) - the main idea is that...; Короче говоря... (KA-ra-che ga-va-RYA) - in short...; Если сказать в двух словах... (YE-slee ska-ZAT v drook sla-VAKH) - to put it in a nutshell... To attribute: По мнению автора... (pa MNYE-nee-yoo A-f ta-ra) - according to the author...; По данным отчёта... (pa DAN-nym at-CHYO-ta) - according to the report's data... To close: В конце автор приходит к выводу, что... (v kan-TSYE A-f tar pree-KHO-deet k VY-va-doo, shta) - in the end the author concludes that... The compression discipline is the hard part. A spoken summary should carry the source's genre and topic, its claim, its main supports, its conclusion, and every hedge and attribution that was doing work in the original. What it must not carry is quotation, ornamental detail, or your own evaluation. A useful test before you speak is to say silently what you are going to leave out, because the omissions are where a summary succeeds or fails. The summary vocabulary is worth fixing as a set rather than word by word: пересказать (pee-ree-ska-ZAT) is to retell, своими словами (sva-EE-mee sla-VA-mee) is in your own words, главное (GLAV-na-ye) is the main thing, суть (SOOT) is the essence, то есть (TO YEST) is that is, and имеется в виду (ee-MYE-yet-sya v vee-DOO) is what is meant is. When you deliberately leave material out, say so: я опускаю детали (ya a-poos-KA-yoo dye-TA-lee), I am leaving out the details.
lessons.example: Here is the remote-work passage from lesson 81, followed by two spoken summaries of it - one bad and one acceptable. The passage: В последние годы многие компании переводят сотрудников на удалённую работу. Сторонники этой практики утверждают, что она экономит время на дорогу. Однако, во-первых, не всякую работу можно делать дома, а во-вторых, дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха. Поэтому, по мнению авторов отчёта, удалённая работа подходит не всем. Bad summary: В последние годы многие компании переводят сотрудников на удалённую работу. Сторонники практики утверждают, что она экономит время на дорогу. Однако, во-первых, не всякую работу можно делать дома, а во-вторых, дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха. (v pas-LYED-nee-ye GO-dy MNO-gee-ye kam-PA-nee pee-ree-VO-dyat so-TROOD-nee-kaf na oo-da-LYON-noo-yoo ra-BO-too. sta-RON-nee-kee PRAK-tee-kee oot-veerzh-DA-yut, shta a-NA e-ka-NO-meet VRYE-mya na da-RO-goo. ad-NA-ka, va-PYER-vykh, nye FSYA-koo-yoo ra-BO-too MOZH-na DYE-lat DO-ma, a va-fta-RYKH, DO-ma TROOD-na at-dee-LEET ra-BO-too at OTD-dy-kha.) Acceptable summary: В тексте говорится о том, что компании всё чаще переводят сотрудников на удалённую работу. По мнению авторов отчёта, у этой практики есть два минуса: не всякую работу можно делать дома, и дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха. Поэтому авторы считают, что удалённая работа подходит не всем. (v TYEK-stye ga-va-REET-sya a TOM, shta kam-PA-nee fsyo CHA-shche pee-ree-VO-dyat so-TROOD-nee-kaf na oo-da-LYON-noo-yoo ra-BO-too. pa MNYE-nee-yoo AF-ta-raf at-CHYO-ta, u EH-tay PRAK-tee-kee yest dva MYE-noo-sa: nye FSYA-koo-yoo ra-BO-too MOZH-na DYE-lat DO-ma, ee DO-ma TROOD-na at-dee-LEET ra-BO-too at OTD-dy-kha. pa-EH-ta-moo AF-ta-ry shchee-TA-yut, shta oo-da-LYON-na-ya ra-BO-ta pad-KHO-deet nye VSYEM.) Compare them. The bad version is four sentences long and verbatim, which is quotation, not summary, and it fails the definition of paraphrase outright; it also drops the final sentence, so it reports the setup and the objections and never reaches the conclusion, which is the part a listener actually needs. The acceptable version is three sentences, replaces the source's words with its own (есть два минуса for во-первых ... во-вторых; всё чаще переводят for многие компании переводят), keeps both attributions (по мнению авторов отчёта, and авторы считают), keeps the double hedge of по мнению, and reaches the conclusion. It uses the то, что frame twice and the по мнению frame in the position where the source had it. Note what it deliberately omits: the phrase В последние годы as a time frame, and the word сторонники, because the report's authors are now the attributed voice. What it must not omit is the attribution, because without it the objections become the speaker's own opinion, which is a different claim. Finally, notice the difference between reporting and evaluating: the acceptable summary never says whether remote work is good. Evaluation is a separate speech act, and mixing it into a summary is the commonest way to be understood as having said something the source did not.
lessons.question: In an oral summary you produce the sentence Дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха. Your listener asks whether this is your opinion or the text's. What is the best Russian repair, and why?
lessons.answer: Re-attribute the claim with a frame: По мнению авторов отчёта, дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха - according to the report's authors, it is hard to separate work from rest at home.
lessons.distractor: Add a hedge of your own: Наверное, дома трудно отделить работу от отдыха - probably it is hard to separate work from rest at home.
lessons.correction: A hedge marks the speaker's confidence; it does not mark whose claim it is. Adding наверное leaves the sentence as your own judgement expressed cautiously, which is exactly the ambiguity the listener is asking about, and it has the extra cost of weakening a claim the source made without hedging. The correct repair is an attribution frame, which moves the claim back to its source: по мнению, по данным, согласно plus a source, or a reporting verb with a что-clause. This is the same equipment you built in lesson 76 for reported speech and in lesson 86 for evidentiality, and a summary is where its absence does the most damage, because there the listener has no source text to check you against.

depth.definitions: Paraphrase: a rewording of a text that retains the original meaning. Abstract: a brief summary of a longer text, often used to let a reader ascertain its purpose, which may stand alone. Gist: the main claim and its principal support, as opposed to the full content. Attribution: language that assigns a claim to a source rather than to the speaker. Cohesion: the grammatical and lexical linking that holds a text together. Reference, ellipsis and substitution: cohesive devices that avoid repetition in the source, which a summariser must usually reverse. Correlative construction: the frame то, что, obligatory with certain verbs and predicative expressions. Reported speech frame: что for a statement, ли for a yes-no question, чтобы for a request, from lesson 76. Prerequisite: lesson 81's argument decomposition, lesson 83's subjectless sentences, lesson 86's evidentiality and hedging, and lesson 76's reporting frames.
depth.mechanism: Summarising aloud is a transformation with a measurable input and output, and the mechanism has four moves. The first is reduction: from the source's sentences you extract one claim, two or three supports and one conclusion, discarding scene-setting and ornamental detail. The second is re-lexicalisation: you replace the source's wording with your own, which is what makes the output a paraphrase rather than a quotation, and this move is also what forces you to understand the content, because you cannot reword what you have not parsed. The third is re-cohesion: the source's referring chains pointed backwards into sentences you have deleted, so you must rebuild them with named nouns, which is why summaries read more repetitively than their sources and why that repetition is correct rather than a fault. The fourth is preservation of stance: every hedge, attribution and modality marker that carried information in the source must survive, because dropping по-видимому or по мнению turns a report into an assertion. This fourth move is the one learners lose, and it is the one that changes meaning rather than style. The limits are worth stating. A summary is not evidence of comprehension on its own: a listener cannot tell whether you understood the text or memorised a plausible-sounding frame, and a teacher needs the source and a follow-up question to check. A spoken summary is also not an abstract in the written sense, because it happens once and unrepeatably, so it must be shorter and more linear than a written abstract of the same text. And there is a real tension between brevity and completeness: a two-sentence summary of a long argument will lose either the support or the attribution, and the professional choice is usually to keep the attribution and cut the support detail, because an unsupported claim correctly attributed is honest whereas a supported claim wrongly owned is not.
depth.secondExample: Take a text of a different type - a short factual notice rather than an argument - and watch the summary routine change shape. Source: В связи с ремонтом эскалаторов с 5 по 12 мая станция метро закрыта для входа. Выход в город возможен через вестибюль номер два. Проезд до соседней станции осуществляется автобусом номер пятнадцать по обычным билетам. (v SVYA-zee s ree-MON-tam es-ka-LA-ta-raf s PYA-ta-va pa dvee-NA-tsa-ta-ye MA-ya STAN-tsee-ya meet-RO zak-RY-ta dlya FKHO-da. VY-khat v GO-rat vaz-MO-zhen CHYE-ryez vees-tee-BYOOL NO-mer dva. pra-YEZD da sa-SYED-nyey STAN-tsee-ee a-soosh-chestv-LYA-yet-sya af-TO-boo-sam NO-mer peet-NA-tsat pa a-BYCH-nym bee-LYE-tam.) - Because of escalator repairs, from 5 to 12 May the metro station is closed for entry. Exit to the city is possible through entrance hall number two. Travel to the neighbouring station is by bus number fifteen on ordinary tickets. Spoken summary: Станция закрыта на вход с пятого по двенадцатое мая из-за ремонта эскалаторов. Выйти можно через второй вестибюль, а до соседней станции довозят автобусом пятнадцать по обычным билетам. (STAN-tsee-ya zak-RY-ta na vkhot s PYA-ta-va pa dvee-NA-tsa-ta-ye MA-ya eez-ZA ree-MON-ta es-ka-LA-ta-raf. VY-tee MOZH-na CHYE-ryez fta-ROY vees-tee-BYOOL, a da sa-SYED-nyey STAN-tsee-ee da-VO-zyat af-TO-boo-sam peet-NA-tsat pa a-BYCH-nym bee-LYE-tam.) Three things changed. The deverbal and bureaucratic frame В связи с ремонтом became the plain conjunction из-за ремонта, which is the register flip from lesson 82 running in the written-to-spoken direction. The passive and impersonal forms закрыта для входа and осуществляется became the active закрыта на вход and the third plural довозят, which is the conversational way of saying someone does it. And the date range and the hall number survived exactly, because in a factual notice the details are the content: a summary that dropped which hall would be a defective summary rather than a brief one. This is the diagnostic that separates the two text types: in an argument you may cut detail, and in a notice you may cut framing but not data.
depth.mistake: The first error is reciting rather than rewording. Learners under pressure reproduce the source's sentences with one or two words changed, and this defeats the purpose twice over: it demonstrates memory rather than understanding, and it produces a summary longer than the original's argument. The diagnostic is to count shared phrases; if the n-grams of your summary match the source's, you have quoted. The second error is losing the attribution, which converts a report into an opinion, as in the repair question above; the fix is a frame, not a hedge. The third error is flattening hedges, so that по-видимому becomes is and маловероятно becomes is not, which turns a cautious source into a confident one. The fourth error is to summarise the topic instead of the argument: Текст о том, как люди работают дома is a title, not a summary, and it conveys none of the claim, the support or the conclusion. The fifth is structural and specific to spoken Russian: using говорить as a reporting verb without что, as in *Автор говорит ремонт начнётся, which is not a Russian sentence; the frame must be говорить, что... or говорить о том, что..., and the correlative with то is obligatory with verbs such as начаться с and with expressions such as доволен.
depth.application: Task: take any one of the reading passages from lessons 81, 83 or 84 - they are all short - and deliver a spoken summary in four sentences: genre and topic, main claim with attribution, the main support, and the conclusion or its relevance to you. Record it, then transcribe it and compare it word by word with the source. Model response for the lesson 83 bridge paragraph: В заметке говорится о ремонте моста в прошлом году. Мост был отремонтирован, причём движение не закрывали. Газеты об этом писали, но точную стоимость работ не сообщили. По данным заметки, теперь на мосту новые фонари. Self-review rubric: (1) are there fewer than five consecutive words shared with the source? (2) does every claim in your summary carry the same attribution and hedging as the source? (3) did you name what you left out? Three yes answers passes. If you answered no to the first, re-record using different words rather than a different summary; the discipline being tested is re-lexicalisation, not recall.
depth.summary: A summary is a paraphrase plus a compression plus an attribution, delivered with its own cohesion rather than the source's. The definitional part - your own words, retained meaning, stand-alone usability - is what separates a summary from a recitation, and the re-cohesion work is why a good summary looks repetitive. In Russian the load-bearing devices are the то, что correlative, the attribution frames по мнению and по данным, and the reporting frames from lesson 76, while the register flip from lesson 82 handles the transformation of bureaucratic written input into spoken output. Keep three limits in view: a summary is not by itself proof of comprehension, a spoken summary must be shorter and more linear than a written abstract, and brevity applied to a factual notice destroys its content rather than compressing it. The final lesson of this level combines everything: a sustained conversation about work, study and plans, in which you summarise, hedge, disagree and sequence for several turns.

steps: Slot 1 - Genre, topic and source. Frame: В тексте говорится о том, что ... / В заметке сообщается о том, что ... Function: tells the listener what kind of text this was and what it is about. Failure it prevents: summarising an opinion piece as if it were a factual notice.

Slot 2 - Main claim with attribution. Frame: По мнению автора, ... / Автор утверждает, что ... Function: carries the proposition and assigns it to its owner. Failure it prevents: the listener hearing the source's claim as your own opinion.

Slot 4 - Conclusion or relevance, and one sentence naming what you left out. Frame: В конце автор приходит к выводу, что ... / Я не пересказываю детали, но ...
